LARK: Learnability-Grounded Trajectory Selection for Efficient Reasoning Distillation

Tianrun Yu, Kaixiang Zhao, Chih-Chun Chen, Amanda Hughes    Taylor W. Killian, Fenglong Ma, Weitong Zhang, Porter Jenkins Affiliation: Brigham Young University  The Pennsylvania State University  University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill *Corresponding author: pjenkins@cs.byu.edu
Abstract

We study trajectory selection for reasoning distillation, where teacher-generated reasoning trajectories are selectively used as supervision for a student model. Existing methods rely on heuristics such as trajectory quality or model confidence, but they often overlook whether a trajectory is learnable by the student. In this paper, we present LARK11 1 Our code is available at https://github.com/Tianrun-Yu/LARK., a learnability-grounded method for reasoning trajectory selection. LARK selects trajectories that the student can learn efficiently while preserving the generalization of the full training distribution. At the core of LARK is a learnability factor ρ\rho, which characterizes the rate at which the student’s training loss decreases. To estimate this rate efficiently and maintain generalization, we introduce a learnability proxy and a χ2\chi^{2}-regularized selection policy that balances learnability and distributional coverage, both with strong theoretical guarantees on their estimation error. Empirically, LARK consistently outperforms data selection baselines across multiple base models and reasoning tasks. Diagnostic analyses show that the LARK score predicts downstream training utility and that LARK-selected trajectories induce faster supervised fine-tuning loss reduction.

1 Introduction

Reasoning distillation has emerged as an effective paradigm for transferring chain-of-thought reasoning abilities from larger teacher Large Language Models (LLMs) to smaller student models (Hsieh et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2023). In this setting, a teacher model generates reasoning trajectories, and a student model is fine-tuned to imitate them. Recent studies have shown that a small set of carefully selected reasoning examples can yield substantial performance gains (Ye et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2025), often rivaling the use of much larger training sets. These findings suggest that reasoning distillation requires both generating sufficient reasoning data and identifying the supervision that is most useful for the student.

Many existing data selection methods for reasoning distillation still inherit the classical formulation of data selection in LLM fine-tuning (Xia et al., 2024; Xiao and Chen, 2025), where selection is performed at the question or sample level (Yu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2024). However, reasoning distillation presents a finer-grained selection problem. For a single question, we often have multiple candidate reasoning trajectories, generated by different teacher models, sampling runs, or reasoning styles. Even when several trajectories lead to the same correct final answer, they may provide very different training signals to the current student model. A trajectory that appears natural, high-quality, or well aligned with the student model is not necessarily the one that the student can learn from most efficiently.

Existing trajectory selection methods largely rely on heuristic criteria. Some methods use external verifiers or LLM-as-a-judge scores to assess reasoning quality (Zheng et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025), while GRAPE, Local Naturalness, and RSR score candidates using the student model itself (Zhang et al., 2025a; Just et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). Although these methods are useful, they do not explicitly measure whether a trajectory is learnable by the student. This gap motivates the central question:

Can we design a principled trajectory selection criterion that ensures
distilled reasoning trajectories are learnable by the student model?

We answer this question by proposing LARK—Learnability-grounded Anchor-time Ranking—a learnability-grounded method for reasoning trajectory selection, as illustrated in Figure 1. LARK identifies the subset of trajectories from which the student model can learn most efficiently. At its core, LARK introduces a principled selection criterion that characterizes trajectory learnability from an optimization perspective, while preserving generalization through χ2\chi^{2}-regularization. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We formulate reasoning trajectory selection as a learnability-grounded policy optimization problem. We introduce the anchor-time learnability rate ρ\rho, which characterizes the decay rate of the post-training loss and thereby turns learnability into a principled optimization objective.

  • •

    To estimate the learnability rate ρ\rho efficiently while preventing the selector from hacking the learnability criterion, we use a first-order Taylor expansion around the unselected data distribution and derive a χ2\chi^{2}-regularized policy optimization problem. Theoretically, we show that this policy optimization implicitly increases data learnability and can be solved in closed form under fixed-budget trajectory selection.

  • •

    Empirically, we show that LARK outperforms existing baselines across multiple base models and tasks. Diagnostic analyses further support our theoretical claims and validate the learnability-grounded perspective for trajectory selection.

Notation.

Vectors are denoted by lowercase boldface letters, e.g., 𝐱\mathbf{x}. For a sequential response, 𝐲<t\mathbf{y}_{<t} denotes the sequence of tokens preceding the tt-th token. We denote by [n][n] the set {1,⋯,n}\{1,\cdots,n\}. For two positive sequences {an}n≥1\{a_{n}\}_{n\geq 1} and {bn}n≥1\{b_{n}\}_{n\geq 1}, we write an=o⁡(bn)a_{n}=o(b_{n}) if an/bn→0a_{n}/b_{n}\to 0 as n→∞n\to\infty. We denote the KK-dimensional simplex by ΔK\Delta^{K}, and ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm throughout the paper. For two distributions pp and qq, the χ2\chi^{2} divergence is defined as χ2(q∥p)=∫x(q(x)−p(x))2/p(x)dx\chi^{2}(q\parallel p)=\int_{x}(q(x)-p(x))^{2}/p(x)\,\mathrm{d}x, with the integral replaced by a summation in the discrete case.

2 Related Work

Reasoning distillation and data selection. Reasoning distillation transfers chain-of-thought traces from stronger teacher models to smaller student models (Hsieh et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2023). Recent work has shown that a small but carefully chosen set of reasoning examples can rival much larger training sets (Yu et al., 2023; Ye et al., 2025; Muennighoff et al., 2025). This has motivated a growing body of work on data-selection methods that filter examples by diversity, difficulty, uncertainty, or learning impact (Zhang et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025).

Most of these methods operate at the question or example level. In contrast, we study a finer-grained problem that arises in reasoning distillation. For a given question, multiple candidate reasoning trajectories may be available. These trajectories can all lead to correct answers while providing substantially different training signals to the student. LARK therefore asks which trajectory, among candidates for the same question, is most learnable for the current student model.

Trajectory selection and optimization-grounded weighting. Existing trajectory-selection methods typically score candidates by either external quality signals or student-side fit. External methods rely on correctness checks, verifiers, or LLM-as-a-judge evaluation to estimate the quality of a reasoning trajectory  (Cobbe et al., 2021). Student-side methods instead use the student model’s own behavior, such as likelihood (GRAPE (Zhang et al., 2025a)), local-context likelihood (Local Naturalness (Just et al., 2025)), or rank-surprisal alignment (RSR (Yang et al., 2026)), to identify trajectories that appear better aligned with the student.

LARK differs from both families by deriving its selection criterion from a local learnability objective. Specifically, it asks whether a trajectory yields a favorable optimization signal for the current student. This perspective connects our work to gradient-based data selection rooted in the Polyak–Łojasiewicz framework (Lojasiewicz, 1963; Karimi et al., 2016; Xia et al., 2024), though unlike those methods we avoid per-trajectory backward passes by using a forward-pass proxy. For multi-trajectory selection, we adopt a χ2\chi^{2}-regularized weighting that is related in spirit to regularized alignment and offline optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2022), yielding a closed-form, budgeted rule.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning for Reasoning Distillation

We consider the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of the student model. Let 𝐱\mathbf{x} be the question and 𝐲k=(y1k,⋯,y|ak|k)⊤\mathbf{y}_{k}{=}(y_{1}^{k},\cdots,y_{|a_{k}|}^{k})^{\top} denote the kk-th trajectory from the teacher with length |ak||a_{k}|. The SFT loss is defined by

ℓ(𝜽,𝐲k)=1|ak|∑t=1|ak|−logπ𝜽(yt∣𝐱,𝐲<t),\displaystyle\textstyle{\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{y}_{k})=\tfrac{1}{|a_{k}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|a_{k}|}-\log\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(y_{t}\mid\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{y}_{<t})},

where π𝜽\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} denotes the student language model with parameter 𝜽\boldsymbol{\theta}. Over a set of response candidates {𝐲k}k=1K\{\mathbf{y}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}, we consider the finite-sum loss over a weight 𝐪=(q1,⋯,qK)⊤\mathbf{q}=(q_{1},\cdots,q_{K})^{\top} written by

ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)=∑k=1Kqk⋅ℓ⁡(𝜽,𝐲k),where ​∑k=1Kqk=1,qk≥0,∀k∈[K],\displaystyle\textstyle{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{q})=\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{k}\cdot\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{y}_{k}),\quad\text{where }\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{k}=1,q_{k}\geq 0,\forall k\in[K]}, (1)

where 𝐪\mathbf{q} encodes which trajectories should be emphasized during the SFT. For instance, when qk=1Kq_{k}=\tfrac{1}{K} for all k∈[K]k\in[K], Eq. (1) reduces to the standard SFT loss over KK trajectories. When BB trajectories are selected for training, it is equivalent to finding a weight vector 𝐪\mathbf{q} on the simplex ΔK\Delta^{K} with the number of non-zero elements exactly equal to BB.

3.2 Gradient Flow Loss Decay Identity

We characterize the learnability from the lens of optimization theory, in which Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) condition of over-parameterized optimization (Bassily et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2022; Chatterjee, 2022) centers on the ratio of the squared gradient norm to the loss. We write this ratio as

ρ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)≜‖∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽,𝐪)‖2/ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐪),\displaystyle\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\triangleq{\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\theta}};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}}/{\mathcal{L}({\boldsymbol{\theta}};\mathbf{q})}, (2)

which we refer to as the loss decay rate function. ρ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{q}) characterizes the landscape of the optimization process. For instance, when ρ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)≥μ\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{q})\geq\mu, Eq. (2) implies ‖∇𝜽ℒ‖2≥μ​ℒ\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}\|^{2}\geq\mu\mathcal{L}, which is commonly used in the analysis of over-parameterized optimization (Liu et al., 2022) (where optimal loss ℒ∗=0\mathcal{L}^{*}{=}0).

Decay rate of gradient flow. Let T>0T>0 denote the total fine-tuning time. For a fixed weight vector 𝐪\mathbf{q}, the gradient flow ϕ𝐪:[0,T]→ℝ|𝜽|\phi_{\mathbf{q}}:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^{|\boldsymbol{\theta}|} describes the evolution of the parameters when the student is fine-tuned on the weighted objective ℒ⁡(⋅,𝐪)\mathcal{L}(\cdot;\,\mathbf{q}), defined as the solution to the ODE

ϕ˙𝐪​(s)=−∇𝜽ℒ​(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪),ϕ𝐪​(0)=𝜽ref,s∈[0,T].\displaystyle\dot{\phi}_{\mathbf{q}}(s)=-\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q}),\qquad\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(0)={\boldsymbol{\theta}}_{\mathrm{ref}},\qquad s\in[0,T].

Here ϕ𝐪​(0)=θref\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(0)=\theta_{\mathrm{ref}} is the starting point of fine-tuning, ϕ𝐪​(T)\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(T) is the parameter at time TT, and ss is the continuous gradient-flow time variable. By the chain rule and Eq.(2), we have

dd​s​ℒ​(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)=−‖∇𝜽ℒ​(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)‖2=−ρ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)​ℒ​(𝜽,𝐪),ϕ𝐪​(0)=θref.\displaystyle\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}s}\mathcal{L}(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})=-\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\|^{2}=-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{q})\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{q}),\quad\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(0)=\theta_{\mathrm{ref}}.

Solving this ordinary differential equation yields

ℒ(ϕ𝐪(T);𝐪)=ℒ(θref;𝐪)⋅exp(−∫0Tρ(ϕ𝐪(s);𝐪)ds),\displaystyle\textstyle{\mathcal{L}(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(T);\mathbf{q})=\mathcal{L}(\theta_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\cdot\exp\left(-\int_{0}^{T}\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\mathrm{d}s\right),} (3)

which implies the integral ∫0Tρ⁡(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)​𝑑s\int_{0}^{T}\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\mathrm{d}s plays an important role in controlling the loss decay.

4 Proposed Method

In this section, we present the methodology of LARK. Specifically, §4.1 establishes that the time-integrated learnability objective in Eq. (3) can be controlled by the anchor-time learnability rate ρ⁡(⋅)\rho(\cdot) evaluated at the initial student model. §4.2 then approximately optimizes ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}) through local linearization around the uniform prior, develops a forward-pass proxy g^k\hat{g}_{k} that estimates the local gradient of ρ\rho without backward propagation, and bounds the residual errors by a χ2\chi^{2}-regularization term to preserve generalization and prevent reward hacking of the learnability criterion. §4.3 combines these pieces into a closed-form, budget-parameterized selection rule with no hyperparameter to tune.

4.1 Estimating the Learnability Objective with Anchor-Relative Condition

As shown in Eq. (3), selecting trajectories that are learnable by the student model can be formulated as optimizing the time-integrated learnability objective max⁡∫0T𝐪∈ΔK⁡ρ⁡(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)​𝑑s\max_{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}}\int_{0}^{T}\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\mathrm{d}s, which favors trajectory distributions under which the post-training loss decays rapidly during SFT. However, directly optimizing this objective is infeasible, since it requires tracking the factor ρ\rho along the entire SFT optimization trajectory. To address this challenge, we introduce the following structural condition, which allows the learnability objective to be approximated from a fixed anchor model.

Condition 1.

We say the model satisfies the anchor-relative condition if there exists an absolute constant κ>0\kappa>0 such that, for every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K} and every s∈[0,T]s\in[0,T], ρ⁡(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)≥κ​ρ​(𝛉ref,𝐪)\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\geq\kappa\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}).

Under Condition 1, the learnability rate evaluated at the initial student parameters 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}} provides a tractable proxy for the full time-integrated objective. This anchor-relative condition is consistent with the lazy fine-tuning behavior often observed in over-parameterized LLMs during SFT. In this regime, the model parameters remain close to the initialization 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}}, and consequently the learnability rate ρ\rho remains close to its anchor-time value ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}). We provide a theoretical justification of this condition under the neural tangent kernel regime (Jacot et al., 2018, NTK;) in Appendix A.2, together with empirical validation in Appendix A.3.

The following proposition then follows naturally; we defer its proof to Appendix A.1.

Proposition 1.

Under Condition 1, for every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}, the post-training loss of the student model satisfies ℒ(ϕ𝐪(T);𝐪)≤ℒ(𝛉ref;𝐪)⋅exp(−κT⋅ρ(𝛉ref;𝐪)).\mathcal{L}(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(T);\mathbf{q})\leq\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\cdot\exp\bigl(-\kappa T\cdot\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\bigr).

Proposition 1 shows that, under the anchor-relative condition, the decay of the SFT loss can be controlled by the learnability rate evaluated at the anchor model 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}}. Therefore, instead of directly optimizing the intractable trajectory-wide objective ∫0Tρ⁡(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)​𝑑s\int_{0}^{T}\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\mathrm{d}s, we can optimize the anchor-time surrogate max𝐪∈ΔK⁡ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\max_{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}) to encourage faster loss decay for the student model.

4.2 Approximately Optimizing Learnability ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}) through Local Linearization

In practice, directly optimizing ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}) is problematic. As shown in Appendix B.1, this objective induces a quasi-convex maximization problem over the simplex ΔK\Delta^{K}, whose optimum is attained at a vertex of the simplex. Consequently, exact maximization would lead to a degenerate solution that places all probability mass on a single trajectory, thereby “hacking” the learnability criterion instead of producing a useful training distribution.

This observation motivates treating the learnability criterion ρ\rho as a local indicator around the uniform distribution 𝐩=(1K,⋯,1K)∈ℝK\mathbf{p}=(\tfrac{1}{K},\cdots,\tfrac{1}{K})\in\mathbb{R}^{K} which corresponds to standard SFT without trajectory selection. Rather than globally maximizing ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}), we restrict attention to distributions 𝐪\mathbf{q} in a neighborhood of 𝐩\mathbf{p} and locally linearize the objective around 𝐩\mathbf{p}. The first-order Taylor expansion gives

ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)−ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)\displaystyle\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{p}) =⟨∇𝐪ρ​(𝜽ref,𝐪),𝐪−𝐩⟩+o⁡(‖𝐪−𝐩‖2)\displaystyle=\textstyle{\langle\nabla_{\mathbf{q}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}),\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p}\rangle+o(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p}\|_{2})}
=∑k=1K∂∂qk​ρ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)∣𝐪=𝐩⏟gk∗⋅(qk−pk)+o⁡(‖𝐪−𝐩‖2)⏟R2​(𝐩,𝐪).\displaystyle=\textstyle{\sum_{k=1}^{K}}\underbrace{\tfrac{\partial}{\partial q_{k}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\mid_{\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p}}}_{g_{k}^{*}}\cdot(q_{k}-p_{k})+\underbrace{o(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p}\|_{2})}_{R_{2}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})}. (4)

Two steps remain for optimizing Eq. (4). First, we need to estimate the first-order derivative gk∗g_{k}^{*} in a computationally efficient manner. Second, we need to bound the residual R2​(𝐩,𝐪)R_{2}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q}) carefully.

4.2.1 Estimating gradient gk∗g_{k}^{*}

According to the definition of ρ\rho, gk∗=∂∂qk​ρ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)=∂∂qk​‖∑iqi​𝐠i‖2∑iqi​ℓig_{k}^{*}=\tfrac{\partial}{\partial q_{k}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})=\tfrac{\partial}{\partial q_{k}}\tfrac{\|\sum_{i}q_{i}\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2}}{\sum_{i}q_{i}\ell_{i}}, where 𝐠i=∇𝜽ℓi\mathbf{g}_{i}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell_{i} and ℓi=ℓ⁡(𝜽,𝐲i)\ell_{i}=\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta},\mathbf{y}_{i}). With detailed derivations deferred to Appendix B.3, we can write

gk∗=2​𝐠k⊤​∑iqi​𝐠i∑iqi​ℓi−‖∑iqi​𝐠i‖2∑jqj​ℓk⋅ℓk∑iqi​ℓi|𝐪=𝐩=2​𝐠k⊤​∑i𝐠i∑iℓi−‖∑i𝐠i‖2∑iℓi⋅ℓk∑iℓi,\displaystyle g_{k}^{*}=\frac{2\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\sum_{i}q_{i}\mathbf{g}_{i}}{\sum_{i}q_{i}\ell_{i}}-\frac{\|\sum_{i}q_{i}\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2}}{\sum_{j}q_{j}\ell_{k}}\cdot\frac{\ell_{k}}{\sum_{i}q_{i}\ell_{i}}\bigg|_{\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p}}=\frac{2\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\sum_{i}\mathbf{g}_{i}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}-\frac{\|\sum_{i}\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}\cdot\frac{\ell_{k}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}, (5)

where the second equality follows from qk=pk=1Kq_{k}=p_{k}=\tfrac{1}{K}. Based on Eq. (5), we make two observations. First, in many practical overparameterized networks, the per-trajectory gradients 𝐠k\mathbf{g}_{k} are nearly orthogonal in high-dimensional parameter space, i.e., 𝐠k⊤​𝐠j≈δj​k​‖𝐠k‖2\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\mathbf{g}_{j}\approx\delta_{jk}\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}. Second, for the single-trajectory ρ\rho-factor defined in Eq. (2), denoted by ρk∗=‖𝐠k‖2/ℓk\rho_{k}^{*}=\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}/\ell_{k}, the gradient norm can be written as ‖𝐠k‖2=ρk∗​ℓk\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}=\rho_{k}^{*}\ell_{k}. Plugging these observations into Eq. (5), gk∗g_{k}^{*} can be approximated by

gk∗≈2​‖𝐠k‖2∑iℓi−∑j‖𝐠j‖2∑iℓi⋅ℓk∑iℓi=ℓk∑iℓi​(2​ρk∗−∑iρi∗​ℓi∑iℓi).\displaystyle g_{k}^{*}\approx\frac{2\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}-\frac{\sum_{j}\|\mathbf{g}_{j}\|^{2}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}\cdot\frac{\ell_{k}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}=\frac{\ell_{k}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}\left(2\rho_{k}^{*}-\frac{\sum_{i}\rho_{i}^{*}\ell_{i}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}\right). (6)

In practice, calculating ρk∗\rho_{k}^{*} requires backward propagation to compute ‖𝐠k‖2\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}, which is computationally expensive at selection time. Fortunately, we can avoid this gradient computation by leveraging the softmax structure of the last layer in next-token prediction, as stated in the following lemma:

Lemma 1 (Forward-pass ρk∗\rho_{k}^{*} estimation, informal).

For any k∈[K]k\in[K], let 𝛑tk∈Δ|𝒱|\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}\in\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|} be the probability vector produced by the student model for the tt-th token, conditioned on the question 𝐱\mathbf{x} and the previous response tokens 𝐲<tk\mathbf{y}_{<t}^{k}, and let 𝛅⁡(ytk)∈Δ|𝒱|\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k})\in\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|} be the one-hot vector corresponding to the ground-truth token from the teacher model. Let ρ^k≜∑t‖𝛑tk−𝛅⁡(ytk)‖2ℓk\hat{\rho}_{k}\triangleq\frac{\sum_{t}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}-\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k})\|^{2}}{\ell_{k}}, then under standard structural conditions, there exist absolute positive constants C1,C2C_{1},C_{2} where ρ^k∈[C1​ρk∗,C2​ρk∗]\hat{\rho}_{k}\in[C_{1}\rho_{k}^{*},C_{2}\rho_{k}^{*}].

Lemma 1 suggests that ρk∗\rho_{k}^{*} can be estimated in a well-controlled manner by the forward-pass quantity ρ^k\hat{\rho}_{k}, without explicitly computing gradients. We defer the detailed proof to Appendix B.4. Substituting ρ^k\hat{\rho}_{k} into Eq. (5) yields our practical estimator of the local gradient:

g^k=ℓk∑iℓi​(2​ρ^k−∑iρ^i​ℓi∑iℓi), where ​ρ^k≜∑t‖𝝅tk−𝜹⁡(ytk)‖2ℓk.\displaystyle\hat{g}_{k}=\frac{\ell_{k}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}\left(2\hat{\rho}_{k}-\frac{\sum_{i}\hat{\rho}_{i}\ell_{i}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}\right),\text{ where }\hat{\rho}_{k}\triangleq\frac{\sum_{t}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}-\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k})\|^{2}}{\ell_{k}}. (7)

4.2.2 Bounding residuals R⁡(𝐩,𝐪)R(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})

We next control the residual errors introduced by the local linearization and the gradient estimation. More precisely, substituting gk∗g_{k}^{*} with g^k\hat{g}_{k} in Eq. (4) yields

ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)−ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)=∑k=1Kg^k⋅(qk−pk)+∑k=1K(gk∗−g^k)⋅(qk−pk)⏟R1​(𝐩,𝐪)+o⁡(‖𝐪−𝐩‖2)⏟R2​(𝐩,𝐪),\displaystyle\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{p})=\textstyle{\sum_{k=1}^{K}}\hat{g}_{k}\cdot(q_{k}-p_{k})+\underbrace{\textstyle{\sum_{k=1}^{K}}(g_{k}^{*}-\hat{g}_{k})\cdot(q_{k}-p_{k})}_{R_{1}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})}+\underbrace{o(\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p}\|_{2})}_{R_{2}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})},

where R1R_{1} captures the error from estimating the true local gradient gk∗g_{k}^{*} by g^k\hat{g}_{k}, and R2R_{2} captures the higher-order error from the Taylor expansion. The following lemma shows that both terms can be controlled by the χ2\chi^{2} distance from the uniform distribution.

Lemma 2 (χ2\chi^{2} controls both error terms, informal).

Under standard structural conditions, there exist constants α1,α2>0\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}>0 such that for all 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K},

|R1(𝐩,𝐪)|≤α1χ2(𝐪∥𝐩)+1,|R2(𝐩,𝐪)|≤α2χ2(𝐪∥𝐩).\displaystyle|R_{1}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})|\leq\alpha_{1}\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\|\mathbf{p})+1,\qquad|R_{2}(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{q})|\leq\alpha_{2}\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\|\mathbf{p}). (8)

Lemma 2 shows that the residual errors are controlled by the χ2\chi^{2} distance between the selected distribution 𝐪\mathbf{q} and the uniform distribution 𝐩\mathbf{p}, with explicit forward-computable constants α1,α2\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2} given in Appendix B.5. This further supports our intuition that optimization should be performed in a local neighborhood around the original, non-selected data distribution 𝐩\mathbf{p}, to preserve generalization and prevent the selector from drifting toward degenerate solutions. Combining the linearized objective with the residual bounds gives the following lower bound on the original learnability improvement; we defer its proof to Appendix B.6.

Theorem 1 (LARK objective, informal).

There exist absolute constants α>0\alpha>0 and C∈ℝC\in\mathbb{R} such that

ρ(𝜽ref;𝐪)−ρ(𝜽ref;𝐩)≥∑k=1Kg^k⋅(qk−pk)−αχ2(𝐪∥𝐩)+C.\displaystyle\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{p})\geq\textstyle{\sum_{k=1}^{K}}\hat{g}_{k}\cdot(q_{k}-p_{k})-\alpha\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\parallel\mathbf{p})+C. (9)

Theorem 1 reduces the intractable learnability improvement to a tractable surrogate that depends on 𝐪\mathbf{q} only through (i) the inner product ⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle between the trajectory deviation and the forward-pass score vector, and (ii) the χ2\chi^{2} distance to the uniform prior. The constant CC is independent of 𝐪\mathbf{q} and therefore does not affect the maximizer over ΔK\Delta^{K}. This reduction sets the stage for the closed-form selection rule developed in §4.3.

4.3 LARK: Closed-form Solution for Fixed-Budget Trajectory Selection

Theorem 1 reduces the intractable learnability improvement to a tractable χ2\chi^{2}-regularized optimization based on {g^k}\{\hat{g}_{k}\}. In practice, many data selection algorithms operate in the fixed-budget setting, where the agent needs to select B≤KB\leq K trajectories per question, meaning that the support size of 𝐪\mathbf{q} is BB. This fixed-budget optimization admits a closed-form solution, as stated in the following lemma.

Lemma 3 (BB-parameterized closed form).

Sort g^1≥⋯≥g^K\hat{g}_{1}\geq\cdots\geq\hat{g}_{K} and assume 1≤B<K1\leq B<K with g^B>g^B+1\hat{g}_{B}>\hat{g}_{B+1}. Under the uniform prior pk=1/Kp_{k}=1/K, the maximizer of optimization objective

𝐪^=argmax𝐪∈ΔK,supp⁡(𝐪)=B{∑k=1Kg^k(qk−pk)−τ⁡(B)2χ2(𝐪∥𝐩)},\displaystyle\hat{\mathbf{q}}=\arg\textstyle{\max_{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K},\mathrm{supp}(\mathbf{q})=B}}\left\{\textstyle\sum\nolimits_{k=1}^{K}\hat{g}_{k}(q_{k}-p_{k})-\tfrac{\tau(B)}{2}\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\|\mathbf{p})\right\}, (10)

with regularizer τ⁡(B)=1K​∑j=1B(g^j−g^B+1)\tau(B)=\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{j=1}^{B}(\hat{g}_{j}-\hat{g}_{B+1}) takes the closed form q^i=(g^i−g^B+1)/∑j=1B(g^j−g^B+1)\hat{q}_{i}=(\hat{g}_{i}-\hat{g}_{B+1})/\sum_{j=1}^{B}(\hat{g}_{j}-\hat{g}_{B+1}) for i≤Bi\leq B, and q^i=0\hat{q}_{i}=0 otherwise.

Lemma 3 gives a closed-form top-BB rule: each selected trajectory is weighted by its score margin above g^B+1\hat{g}_{B+1}, and τ∗​(B)\tau^{*}(B) is fully determined by BB with no hyperparameter to tune. Algorithm 1 summarizes the full procedure.

Remark 1 (Soft vs. hard top-BB).

LARK is a soft top-BB rule: weights are proportional to score margins above the threshold, rather than uniform 1/B1/B as in hard top-BB truncation. This hedges against ranking noise near the boundary; the ablation in §5.3 (Figure 2(b)) shows it outperforms uniform, proportional, and softmax weighting.

Remark 2 (Heuristic reading of g^k\hat{g}_{k}).

g^k\hat{g}_{k} favors trajectories on which the student is confidently wrong in a structured way: ℓk\ell_{k} is not small, indicating that the student does not yet predict it well, yet the residual mass ‖𝝅tk−𝜹⁡(ytk)‖2\|\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}-\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k})\|^{2} concentrates on a few near-miss tokens, providing a clear local correction signal. Although g^k\hat{g}_{k} is a forward-pass surrogate for the exact directional derivative gk∗g_{k}^{*}, the two remain tightly aligned: Appendix B.8 gives an explicit error bound on ‖𝐠^−𝐠∗‖𝐩\|\hat{\mathbf{g}}-\mathbf{g}^{*}\|_{\mathbf{p}} and verifies it on real student models, while the token-level signature is verified in §5.4 (Figure 4).

5 Experiment

We evaluate LARK on reasoning distillation through three research questions. RQ1 asks whether LARK outperforms heuristic, quality-based, and student-side baselines under single-trajectory (B=1B{=}1) and multi-trajectory (B=3B{=}3) supervision. RQ2 isolates the contribution of the trajectory score g^k\hat{g}_{k} and the χ2\chi^{2}-BB weighting rule by holding one fixed and varying the other. RQ3 asks why LARK works, by linking g^k\hat{g}_{k} to the anchor-time learnability rate ρ\rho, to the SFT loss trajectory, and to downstream training utility, and by analyzing the token-level structure of the trajectories LARK selects. Section 5.1 describes the shared experimental setup, and Sections 5.2–5.4 answer each question in turn.

5.1 Experimental Setup

Candidate pool. We use a fixed set of 5,0005{,}000 math problems from NuminaMath (Li et al., 2024), each paired with 3333 trajectories from 1111 teacher models (33 rollouts each); see Appendix C.1. All methods share this pool, so any performance difference reflects the selection rule alone.

Selection budgets. We evaluate each method at B=1B{=}1 (single trajectory per problem) and B=3B{=}3 (three trajectories). Baselines take the top-BB under their score with uniform weights 1/B1/B; LARK applies the χ2\chi^{2}-BB rule of Lemma 3 to obtain weighted 𝐪^\hat{\mathbf{q}} from g^k\hat{g}_{k} computed at the reference student 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}}.

Baselines. We compare LARK against seven methods (Appendix C.2) spanning heuristics, quality-based selection, LLM-based evaluation, and student-side forward-pass scoring: Random, Token Lengthmax, Rule-based Qualitymax, LLM-judged Qualitymax, GRAPEmax (Zhang et al., 2025a), Local Naturalnessmax (Just et al., 2025), and RSRmin (Yang et al., 2026).

Students, training, evaluation. We fine-tune Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-2.5-1.5B (Yang et al., 2024), and Llama-3.2-3B (Grattafiori et al., 2024) via SFT, and evaluate on AIME-2024 (, 2024), AMC (Mathematical Association of America, 2025), GPQA-Diamond (Rein et al., 2024), and MATH-500 (Hendrycks et al., 2021) using Acc@5 (55 samples per problem, marked correct if any contains the gold answer). For each method, we run inference under three independent decoding seeds using the corresponding trained checkpoint and evaluation protocol for that method; we report mean±\pmstd across these three decoding seeds, so the reported variability reflects inference-time sampling rather than training-seed noise. The Avg column in Table 1 is the unweighted mean across the four benchmarks; per-benchmark numbers are the primary basis of comparison. A train/eval contamination audit appears in Appendix C.5. Training and decoding details are in Appendices C.3–C.4.

5.2 RQ1: Does LARK Outperform Existing Trajectory Selection Methods?

Table 1 compares LARK with all baselines on three students. LARK achieves the best average Acc@5 in all six model-budget settings. On Qwen-2.5-7B, it improves over the strongest baseline RSR by 7.167.16 points at B=1B{=}1 and 7.077.07 points at B=3B{=}3, with large gains on AMC and GPQA. The consistent gains under both budgets suggest that LARK improves trajectory quality, not only supervision size. The same trend holds for smaller students: LARK reaches 41.09%41.09\% / 43.14%43.14\% on Qwen-2.5-1.5B and 26.29%26.29\% / 29.13%29.13\% on Llama-3.2-3B under B=1B{=}1 / B=3B{=}3, suggesting that the score is not tied to one student family or scale. Appendix D.2 provides a budget-scaling analysis for LARK across B∈{1,3,5,10,20}B\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}.

5.3 RQ2: How Much Does Each Component Contribute?

We ablate the two design choices in LARK: the trajectory score and the weighting rule.

Trajectory score. Fixing the weighting to χ2\chi^{2}-BB, we compare four scores (Figure 2(a)): the inverse loss 1/ℓk1/\ell_{k}, the Brier residual ∑t‖𝝅tk−𝜹⁡(ytk)‖2\sum_{t}\|\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}-\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k})\|^{2}, the proxy ρ^k\hat{\rho}_{k} of Lemma 1, and the induced score g^k\hat{g}_{k}. The inverse loss is the weakest, confirming that likelihood alone does not characterize learnability; ρ^k\hat{\rho}_{k} already improves substantially by combining residual error with loss; and g^k\hat{g}_{k} is the best across all four benchmarks, since it captures the marginal contribution of each trajectory around 𝐩\mathbf{p} rather than scoring trajectories in isolation.

Weighting rule. Fixing the score to g^k\hat{g}_{k}, we vary the weighting at B=3B{=}3 (Figure 2(b)) over uniform, score-proportional, softmax, and χ2\chi^{2}-BB weights. The χ2\chi^{2}-BB rule consistently outperforms the alternatives, with the largest gains on AIME (where score noise matters most) and on MATH-500 (where the benefit accumulates over many problems). LARK’s improvement therefore comes not only from selecting high-g^k\hat{g}_{k} trajectories but also from assigning robust weights within the selected support.

Efficiency. LARK is forward-pass only and therefore does not require the per-trajectory backward passes needed to compute the exact directional derivative gk∗g_{k}^{*}. Its scoring cost matches the lowest-cost student-side baselines, with full complexity analysis and wall-clock measurements reported in Appendix D.1.

5.4 RQ3: Why Does LARK Work?

We provide three pieces of evidence connecting g^k\hat{g}_{k} to the quantities it is designed to control, then characterize what makes the trajectories LARK selects informative.

g^k\hat{g}_{k} controls the anchor-time learnability rate. We first verify that maximizing g^k\hat{g}_{k} actually raises ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}), the quantity LARK is designed to optimize (§4.1). For a representative problem we evaluate Δ​ρ​(𝐪)=ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)−ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)\Delta\rho(\mathbf{q})=\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{p}) densely over ΔK\Delta^{K} and project onto two PCA components (Figure 3a). The LARK selections 𝐪^​(B)\hat{\mathbf{q}}(B) for B∈{1,…,32}B\in\{1,\ldots,32\} trace a path through the Δ​ρ>0\Delta\rho>0 region (green) and avoid the Δ​ρ<0\Delta\rho<0 region (red): every 𝐪^​(B)\hat{\mathbf{q}}(B) satisfies ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪^​(B))≥ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\hat{\mathbf{q}}(B))\geq\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{p}). The forward-pass surrogate therefore acts as an effective control on the underlying anchor-time learnability rate on real student models.

High g^k\hat{g}_{k} yields faster SFT loss decay. By Proposition 1, a higher ρ\rho should translate into faster SFT loss decay. We verify this by tracking Δ​ℒt≜ℒt−ℒ0\Delta\mathcal{L}_{t}\triangleq\mathcal{L}_{t}-\mathcal{L}_{0} on Qwen-2.5-7B at B=3B{=}3. Figure 3b shows that LARK achieves the largest loss reduction throughout training, with the gap visible already in the early stage; heuristic and naturalness baselines reduce the loss more slowly and converge to a shallower plateau, even when starting from a lower initial loss.

g^k\hat{g}_{k} predicts downstream training utility. We finally check that g^k\hat{g}_{k} tracks downstream Acc@5 in practice. We group the 3333 candidates by their teacher model (1111 teachers), fine-tune Qwen-2.5-7B separately on each teacher’s trajectories, and evaluate on AMC. The per-teacher mean of g^k\hat{g}_{k} is strongly correlated with downstream AMC accuracy (Figure 3c, Pearson r=0.69r=0.69, p=0.018p=0.018): high-g^k\hat{g}_{k} teachers (GPT-OSS-20B/120B, Phi-4-R+, QwQ-32B) yield students above 65%65\%, while low-g^k\hat{g}_{k} teachers (Magistral-S, Nemotron) yield students below 55%55\%. The score is predictively valid at the teacher level, capturing a student-side training signal that surface quality and likelihood do not.

Mechanism: confidently wrong, in a structured way. The three results above establish that maximizing g^k\hat{g}_{k} raises ρ\rho, accelerates SFT loss decay, and predicts utility, but do not explain why the selected trajectories carry strong signal. We compute under 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}} two token-level statistics for each candidate: the mean correct-token probability p¯​(yt)\bar{p}(y_{t}), and the wrong-token concentration ∑v≠ytp​(v)2\sum_{v\neq y_{t}}p(v)^{2}, which is large when the residual mass falls on a few wrong tokens. Comparing all 33×50033\times 500 candidates with the LARK-selected top-11 (Figure 4), the selected trajectories have substantially lower p¯​(yt)\bar{p}(y_{t}) (0.2820.282 vs. 0.4490.449) and higher wrong-token concentration (0.1070.107 vs. 0.0850.085, a 26%26\% increase). LARK therefore avoids trajectories the student already predicts confidently and routes supervision toward trajectories on which the student is wrong but in a structured way: residual mass concentrates on near-miss tokens close to the gold answer, providing a clear local correction signal. This signature echoes the rank-based view of RSR (Yang et al., 2026), which detects token positions where the gold answer is a near-miss, and clarifies why LARK and RSR end up close in Table 1 despite arising from distinct theoretical objectives. A single-problem walkthrough is given in Appendix D.3.

6 Conclusion

We presented LARK, a learnability-grounded method for reasoning trajectory selection in distillation. LARK estimates trajectory learnability with a forward-pass surrogate g^k\hat{g}_{k} and uses a closed-form χ2\chi^{2}-regularized soft top-BB rule to construct a weighted SFT objective, avoiding expensive per-trajectory backward passes while preserving distributional coverage. Across three student models and four reasoning benchmarks, LARK consistently outperforms strong trajectory selection baselines under both single-trajectory and multi-trajectory budgets. Ablation and diagnostic analyses show that both the learnability score and the weighting rule are important, and that LARK-selected trajectories accelerate SFT loss decay while providing structured local correction signals. Overall, our results support learnability as an effective principle for efficient reasoning distillation, with future extensions to noisier candidate pools and broader reasoning domains.

Appendix A Anchor-Time Analysis of the Learnability Objective

This appendix supports the anchor-time reduction in Section 4.1. We first prove the post-training loss bound (Appendix A.1). We then provide a theoretical justification of the anchor-relative trajectory bound through the NTK lazy-training framework (Appendix A.2), and verify it empirically on real SFT trajectories (Appendix A.3).

A.1 Proof of the Anchor-Time Loss Decay Bound

Proof of Proposition 1.

Fix any 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}. By the gradient-flow decay identity (3) and Condition 1, which gives ρ⁡(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)≥κ⋅ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\geq\kappa\cdot\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}) for every s∈[0,T]s\in[0,T], we have

∫0Tρ⁡(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)​𝑑s≥∫0Tκ⋅ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)​𝑑s=κ​T⋅ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪).\int_{0}^{T}\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\,ds\;\geq\;\int_{0}^{T}\kappa\cdot\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\,ds\;=\;\kappa T\cdot\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}).

Substituting into (3) and using the non-negativity of ℒ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}) together with the monotonicity of x↦exp⁡(−x)x\mapsto\exp(-x) on ℝ\mathbb{R},

ℒ(ϕ𝐪(T);𝐪)=ℒ(𝜽ref;𝐪)⋅exp(−∫0Tρ(ϕ𝐪(s);𝐪)ds)≤ℒ(𝜽ref;𝐪)⋅exp(−κT⋅ρ(𝜽ref;𝐪)).\mathcal{L}(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(T);\mathbf{q})\;=\;\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\cdot\exp\!\left(-\int_{0}^{T}\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\,ds\right)\;\leq\;\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\cdot\exp\!\bigl(-\kappa T\cdot\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\bigr). (11)

Since 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K} was arbitrary, the bound holds for every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}. ∎

A.2 NTK-Based Justification of the Trajectory Bound

We provide a theoretical justification of Condition 1 through the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) framework. Under standard NTK lazy-training conditions for pretrained language model fine-tuning, combined with a local non-degeneracy condition on the ground-truth probability, we derive a strictly positive constant κ\kappa for which Condition 1 provably holds.

Note on terminology.

Throughout this subsection, we distinguish between two kinds of structural premises. Condition 1 is the anchor-relative condition stated in the main text, which we aim to justify. Assumptions A.1–A.4 below are standard NTK lazy-training premises, which we use to derive Condition 1 as a theorem (Proposition 2).

NTK setup.

We adopt the token-level objects from Section 4.2. For each candidate trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k}, recall the per-token residual δt=πt−𝐞yt∈ℝV\delta_{t}=\pi_{t}-\mathbf{e}_{y_{t}}\in\mathbb{R}^{V} and the stacked residual matrix Δk=[δ1,…,δ|ak|]⊤∈ℝ|ak|×V\Delta_{k}=[\delta_{1},\ldots,\delta_{|a_{k}|}]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{|a_{k}|\times V}, with pt=πt​(yt)p_{t}=\pi_{t}(y_{t}) the probability assigned to the ground-truth token. We additionally introduce the following appendix-only objects.

Logits Jacobian. For trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k}, define

Jk​(𝜽)≜∂∂𝜽​vec​(𝐳1,…,𝐳|ak|)∈ℝ|ak|​V×|𝜽|.J_{k}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\triangleq\frac{\partial}{\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}}\,\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{z}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{z}_{|a_{k}|})\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{|a_{k}|V\times|\boldsymbol{\theta}|}. (12)

Vectorized residual. Let 𝚫k​(𝜽)≜vec⁡(Δk​(𝜽))∈ℝ|ak|​V\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{k}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\triangleq\mathrm{vec}(\Delta_{k}(\boldsymbol{\theta}))\in\mathbb{R}^{|a_{k}|V}.

Weighted NTK matrix and weighted residual. Given 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}, let

J~​(𝜽,𝐪)≜(q1/|a1|​J1​(𝜽)qK/|aK|​JK​(𝜽)),𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)≜(q1/|a1|​𝚫1​(𝜽)qK/|aK|​𝚫K​(𝜽)),\tilde{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\triangleq\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{q_{1}/|a_{1}|}\,J_{1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\\ \vdots\\ \sqrt{q_{K}/|a_{K}|}\,J_{K}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\end{pmatrix},\qquad\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\triangleq\begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{q_{1}/|a_{1}|}\,\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{1}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\\ \vdots\\ \sqrt{q_{K}/|a_{K}|}\,\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{K}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\end{pmatrix}, (13)

and define the weighted empirical NTK matrix

Θ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)≜J~​(𝜽,𝐪)​J~​(𝜽,𝐪)⊤.\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\triangleq\tilde{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\,\tilde{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})^{\top}. (14)

NTK identity. By the standard chain rule for softmax cross-entropy (∇𝐳tℓt=δt\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\ell_{t}=\delta_{t}, see Section 4.2), the weighted gradient admits the factorization

∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽,𝐪)=J~​(𝜽,𝐪)⊤​𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪),\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})=\tilde{J}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})^{\top}\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q}),

which yields the NTK identity

‖∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽,𝐪)‖2=𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)⊤​Θ​(𝜽,𝐪)​𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪).\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}\;=\;\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})^{\top}\,\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q}). (15)

When some qk=0q_{k}=0, the corresponding trajectory block contributes neither to the weighted loss nor to its gradient. The zero-weight blocks are therefore harmless in the identity above, but they should not be used to impose full-matrix positive definiteness. This is why Assumption A.3 below conditions the NTK only along the residual directions that enter the weighted objective.

Assumptions.

We adopt four conditions for the NTK analysis of language model fine-tuning.

Assumption A.1 (Lazy training).

There exists a constant R>0R>0 such that, for every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K},

sups∈[0,T]‖ϕ𝐪​(s)−𝜽ref‖≤R.\sup_{s\in[0,T]}\|\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s)-\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|\;\leq\;R. (16)
Assumption A.2 (NTK stability).

There exists ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1) such that, for every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K} and every 𝜽∈B⁡(𝜽ref,R)\boldsymbol{\theta}\in B(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}},R),

(1−ϵ)​Θ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)⪯Θ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)⪯(1+ϵ)​Θ​(𝜽ref,𝐪).(1-\epsilon)\,\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\;\preceq\;\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\;\preceq\;(1+\epsilon)\,\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}). (17)
Assumption A.3 (Residual-direction NTK conditioning at anchor).

There exist constants 0<λ−≤λ+<∞0<\lambda_{-}\leq\lambda_{+}<\infty such that, for every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K} and every 𝜽∈B⁡(𝜽ref,R)\boldsymbol{\theta}\in B(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}},R),

𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)⊤​Θ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)​𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)≥λ−​‖𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)‖2,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})^{\top}\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\;\geq\;\lambda_{-}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}, (18)

and

𝚫~​(𝜽ref,𝐪)⊤​Θ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)​𝚫~​(𝜽ref,𝐪)≤λ+​‖𝚫~​(𝜽ref,𝐪)‖2.\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})^{\top}\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\;\leq\;\lambda_{+}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}. (19)
Assumption A.4 (Bounded ground-truth probability).

There exist constants 0<p−≤p+<10<p_{-}\leq p_{+}<1 such that, for every 𝜽∈B⁡(𝜽ref,R)\boldsymbol{\theta}\in B(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}},R), every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}, every k∈[K]k\in[K], and every token position tt,

p−≤pt​(𝜽)≤p+.p_{-}\;\leq\;p_{t}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\;\leq\;p_{+}. (20)

Assumption A.1 encodes lazy fine-tuning behavior, classical in NTK theory [Jacot et al., 2018, Chizat et al., 2019] and supported empirically for pre-trained transformer fine-tuning by Malladi et al. [2023]. Assumption A.2 requires the empirical NTK matrix to remain near-constant within the lazy ball, with rate O⁡(1/m)O(1/\sqrt{m}) at width mm [Lee et al., 2019, Jacot et al., 2018], and is supported empirically by Malladi et al. [2023] for fine-tuning. Assumption A.3 is a residual-direction conditioning condition: it does not require the full weighted NTK matrix to be positive definite in directions corresponding to zero-weight trajectories, but only requires non-degenerate curvature along the residual directions that determine the weighted loss and its gradient. Assumption A.4 is a local non-degeneracy condition on teacher-forced token probabilities: pt>0p_{t}>0 holds strictly under finite logits, while pt<1p_{t}<1 excludes already-converged tokens for which the residual signal vanishes.

Loss-residual relation.

Before establishing the main result, we relate the loss ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q}) to the squared residual norm ‖𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)‖2\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}. The relation depends only on Assumption A.4, and the constants ν−,ν+\nu_{-},\nu_{+} are derived explicitly from p−,p+p_{-},p_{+}.

Lemma 4 (Loss–residual two-sided bound).

Under Assumption A.4, for every 𝛉∈B⁡(𝛉ref,R)\boldsymbol{\theta}\in B(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}},R) and every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K},

ν−​‖𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)‖2≤ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)≤ν+​‖𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)‖2,\nu_{-}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}\;\leq\;\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\;\leq\;\nu_{+}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}, (21)

where

ν−=12,ν+=log⁡(1/p−)(1−p+)2.\nu_{-}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{2},\qquad\nu_{+}\;=\;\frac{\log(1/p_{-})}{(1-p_{+})^{2}}. (22)
Proof.

We first establish corresponding pointwise bounds at the token level: for every token position tt, with p≜pt∈[p−,p+]p\triangleq p_{t}\in[p_{-},p_{+}],

12​‖δt‖2≤ℓt≤log⁡(1/p−)(1−p+)2​‖δt‖2.\tfrac{1}{2}\,\|\delta_{t}\|^{2}\;\leq\;\ell_{t}\;\leq\;\frac{\log(1/p_{-})}{(1-p_{+})^{2}}\,\|\delta_{t}\|^{2}. (23)
