‖δt‖2\displaystyle\|\delta_{t}\|^{2} =(a)(1−p)2+∑v≠ytπt​(v)2\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{=}}(1-p)^{2}+\sum_{v\neq y_{t}}\pi_{t}(v)^{2}
≤(b)(1−p)2+(maxv≠yt⁡πt​(v))​∑v≠ytπt​(v)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{\leq}}(1-p)^{2}+\Bigl(\max_{v\neq y_{t}}\pi_{t}(v)\Bigr)\sum_{v\neq y_{t}}\pi_{t}(v)
≤(c)(1−p)2+(1−p)⋅(1−p)= 2​(1−p)2\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(c)}}{{\leq}}(1-p)^{2}+(1-p)\cdot(1-p)\;=\;2(1-p)^{2}
≤(d)2​(1−p)≤(e)2​ℓt,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{\leq}}2(1-p)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(e)}}{{\leq}}2\ell_{t}, (24)

where (a) is the definition δt=πt−𝐞yt\delta_{t}=\pi_{t}-\mathbf{e}_{y_{t}} together with πt​(yt)=p\pi_{t}(y_{t})=p; (b) uses ∑vav2≤maxv⁡av⋅∑vav\sum_{v}a_{v}^{2}\leq\max_{v}a_{v}\cdot\sum_{v}a_{v} for non-negative {av}\{a_{v}\}; (c) uses both maxv≠yt⁡πt​(v)≤∑v≠ytπt​(v)=1−p\max_{v\neq y_{t}}\pi_{t}(v)\leq\sum_{v\neq y_{t}}\pi_{t}(v)=1-p and ∑v≠ytπt​(v)=1−p\sum_{v\neq y_{t}}\pi_{t}(v)=1-p; (d) uses 1−p≤11-p\leq 1; and (e) uses the elementary inequality −log⁡p≥1−p-\log p\geq 1-p for p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1].

Upper bound.

ℓt\displaystyle\ell_{t} =(f)−log⁡p≤(g)log⁡(1/p−)\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(f)}}{{=}}-\log p\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(g)}}{{\leq}}\log(1/p_{-})
=(h)log⁡(1/p−)(1−p+)2​(1−p+)2≤(i)log⁡(1/p−)(1−p+)2​(1−p)2≤(j)log⁡(1/p−)(1−p+)2​‖δt‖2,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(h)}}{{=}}\frac{\log(1/p_{-})}{(1-p_{+})^{2}}\,(1-p_{+})^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(i)}}{{\leq}}\frac{\log(1/p_{-})}{(1-p_{+})^{2}}\,(1-p)^{2}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(j)}}{{\leq}}\frac{\log(1/p_{-})}{(1-p_{+})^{2}}\,\|\delta_{t}\|^{2}, (25)

where (f) is the definition of ℓt\ell_{t}; (g) uses p≥p−p\geq p_{-} and the monotonicity of −log-\log; (h) is multiplication and division by (1−p+)2>0(1-p_{+})^{2}>0; (i) uses (1−p+)2≤(1−p)2(1-p_{+})^{2}\leq(1-p)^{2} from p≤p+<1p\leq p_{+}<1; and (j) uses ‖δt‖2≥(1−p)2\|\delta_{t}\|^{2}\geq(1-p)^{2} from the yty_{t}-th coordinate.

Aggregation. Summing (23) over t=1,…,|ak|t=1,\ldots,|a_{k}| and dividing by |ak||a_{k}| yields

ν−​‖𝚫k‖2/|ak|≤ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐲k)≤ν+​‖𝚫k‖2/|ak|,\nu_{-}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{k}\|^{2}/|a_{k}|\leq\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{y}_{k})\leq\nu_{+}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{k}\|^{2}/|a_{k}|,

where ‖𝚫k‖2=∑t‖δt‖2\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{k}\|^{2}=\sum_{t}\|\delta_{t}\|^{2}. Multiplying by qkq_{k} and summing over kk gives

ν−​∑k=1Kqk|ak|​‖𝚫k‖2≤ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)≤ν+​∑k=1Kqk|ak|​‖𝚫k‖2,\nu_{-}\,\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{q_{k}}{|a_{k}|}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{k}\|^{2}\;\leq\;\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\;\leq\;\nu_{+}\,\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{q_{k}}{|a_{k}|}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{k}\|^{2}, (26)

and the result follows from

∑k(qk/|ak|)​‖𝚫k‖2=‖𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)‖2.\sum_{k}(q_{k}/|a_{k}|)\,\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}_{k}\|^{2}=\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}.

∎

Main result.

We now establish the main result.

Proposition 2 (NTK-based justification of Condition 1).

Under Assumptions A.1–A.4, Condition 1 holds with

κ=(1−ϵ)​λ−​ν−λ+​ν+=(1−ϵ)​λ−​(1−p+)22​λ+​log⁡(1/p−)> 0.\kappa\;=\;\frac{(1-\epsilon)\,\lambda_{-}\,\nu_{-}}{\lambda_{+}\,\nu_{+}}\;=\;\frac{(1-\epsilon)\,\lambda_{-}\,(1-p_{+})^{2}}{2\,\lambda_{+}\,\log(1/p_{-})}\;>\;0. (27)
Proof.

Fix any 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K} and s∈[0,T]s\in[0,T], and set 𝜽=ϕ𝐪​(s)\boldsymbol{\theta}=\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s). Assumption A.1 gives 𝜽∈B⁡(𝜽ref,R)\boldsymbol{\theta}\in B(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}},R).

Writing 𝚫~≜𝚫~​(𝜽,𝐪)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}\triangleq\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q}),

‖∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽,𝐪)‖2\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\|^{2} =(a)𝚫~⊤​Θ​(𝜽,𝐪)​𝚫~\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{=}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}^{\top}\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}
≥(b)(1−ϵ)​𝚫~⊤​Θ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)​𝚫~\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{\geq}}(1-\epsilon)\,\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}^{\top}\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}
≥(c)(1−ϵ)​λ−​‖𝚫~‖2,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(c)}}{{\geq}}(1-\epsilon)\,\lambda_{-}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}\|^{2}, (28)

where (a) is the NTK identity (15); (b) applies the lower-bound part of Assumption A.2; and (c) applies the residual-direction lower bound (18) from Assumption A.3. Combined with the upper bound ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)≤ν+​‖𝚫~‖2\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\leq\nu_{+}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}\|^{2} from Lemma 4,

ρ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)=‖∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽,𝐪)‖2ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐪)≥(1−ϵ)​λ−​‖𝚫~‖2ν+​‖𝚫~‖2=(1−ϵ)​λ−ν+.\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\;=\;\frac{\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}}{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{q})}\;\geq\;\frac{(1-\epsilon)\,\lambda_{-}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}\|^{2}}{\nu_{+}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}\|^{2}}\;=\;\frac{(1-\epsilon)\,\lambda_{-}}{\nu_{+}}. (29)

Writing 𝚫~ref≜𝚫~​(𝜽ref,𝐪)\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_{\mathrm{ref}}\triangleq\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}),

‖∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)‖2\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\|^{2} =(d)𝚫~ref⊤​Θ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)​𝚫~ref\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_{\mathrm{ref}}^{\top}\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_{\mathrm{ref}}
≤(e)λ+​‖𝚫~ref‖2,\displaystyle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(e)}}{{\leq}}\lambda_{+}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|^{2}, (30)

where (d) is (15) at 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}} and (e) applies the residual-direction upper bound (19) from Assumption A.3. Combined with the lower bound ℒ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)≥ν−​‖𝚫~ref‖2\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\geq\nu_{-}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|^{2} from Lemma 4,

ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)=‖∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)‖2ℒ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)≤λ+​‖𝚫~ref‖2ν−​‖𝚫~ref‖2=λ+ν−.\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\;=\;\frac{\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})\|^{2}}{\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})}\;\leq\;\frac{\lambda_{+}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|^{2}}{\nu_{-}\,\|\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Delta}}_{\mathrm{ref}}\|^{2}}\;=\;\frac{\lambda_{+}}{\nu_{-}}. (31)

Combining (29) and (31), both being positive,

ρ​(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)≥(f)(1−ϵ)​λ−/ν+λ+/ν−=(1−ϵ)​λ−​ν−λ+​ν+,\frac{\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})}{\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(f)}}{{\geq}}\;\frac{(1-\epsilon)\,\lambda_{-}/\nu_{+}}{\lambda_{+}/\nu_{-}}\;=\;\frac{(1-\epsilon)\,\lambda_{-}\,\nu_{-}}{\lambda_{+}\,\nu_{+}}, (32)

where (f) uses the lower bound on the numerator from (29) and the upper bound on the denominator from (31). Since 𝐪\mathbf{q} and ss were arbitrary,

infs∈[0,T]ρ⁡(ϕ𝐪​(s),𝐪)≥(1−ϵ)​λ−​ν−λ+​ν+⋅ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪),\inf_{s\in[0,T]}\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{q}}(s);\mathbf{q})\;\geq\;\frac{(1-\epsilon)\,\lambda_{-}\,\nu_{-}}{\lambda_{+}\,\nu_{+}}\cdot\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}), (33)

which is Condition 1 with

κ=(1−ϵ)​λ−​ν−λ+​ν+.\kappa=\frac{(1-\epsilon)\lambda_{-}\nu_{-}}{\lambda_{+}\nu_{+}}.

Substituting ν−=1/2\nu_{-}=1/2 and ν+=log⁡(1/p−)/(1−p+)2\nu_{+}=\log(1/p_{-})/(1-p_{+})^{2} from Lemma 4 yields (27). ∎

Remark on κ\kappa.

The expression

κ=(1−ϵ)​λ−​(1−p+)22​λ+​log⁡(1/p−)\kappa=\frac{(1-\epsilon)\lambda_{-}(1-p_{+})^{2}}{2\lambda_{+}\log(1/p_{-})}

admits a clean interpretation. The ratio λ−/λ+\lambda_{-}/\lambda_{+} is the effective condition number of the empirical NTK along the residual directions that determine the weighted loss; 1−ϵ1-\epsilon captures NTK stability along the trajectory; and (1−p+)2/log⁡(1/p−)(1-p_{+})^{2}/\log(1/p_{-}) is a geometric correction accounting for the cross-entropy loss, arising from the unbounded growth of −log⁡p-\log p near p=0p=0. Under squared loss, this last factor reduces to a constant and κ\kappa collapses to (1−ϵ)​λ−/λ+(1-\epsilon)\lambda_{-}/\lambda_{+}, recovering the classical NTK convergence-rate dependence on the kernel condition number [Jacot et al., 2018, Du et al., 2019]. The post-training loss bound in Proposition 1 thus holds with this κ\kappa, providing theoretical justification for using ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q}) as the anchor-time selection objective in Section 4.1.

A.3 Empirical Verification of the Trajectory Bound

Experimental setup.

Condition 1 quantifies over all 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}, with no restriction on the candidate pool of the weighted SFT loss in Eq. (1): the pool may consist of the KK trajectories of a single question, or of (question, trajectory) pairs aggregated across multiple questions. In actual deployment, LARK is not applied to a single question in isolation but to mini-batches drawn from a corpus of questions, where each batch induces a weight vector over the (question, trajectory) pairs it contains. We therefore verify Condition 1 directly in the corpus-level regime in which LARK is deployed.

Model and anchor. We verify on Qwen-2.5-7B, the main student model used in Section 5.1. The pre-trained checkpoint serves as the anchor parameter 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}}.

Verification corpus. From the 5,000 NuminaMath training questions used in Section 5.1, we randomly sample 500 questions {𝐱n}n=1500\{\mathbf{x}_{n}\}_{n=1}^{500} as the verification corpus. Each 𝐱n\mathbf{x}_{n} retains its full pool of 33 candidate trajectories (11 teachers ×\times 3 rollouts). For each 𝐱n\mathbf{x}_{n} and each budget B∈{1,3,5,10,20}B\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}, we apply the LARK selection rule (Lemma 3) to obtain a weight vector 𝐪^n(B)\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{n}^{(B)}. Stacking and rescaling the 500500 per-question weights yields a corpus-level weight vector 𝐐(B)∈Δ500×33\mathbf{Q}^{(B)}\in\Delta^{500\times 33}, with the corresponding weighted SFT loss

ℒtotal​(𝜽,B)≜ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐐(B))=1500​∑n=1500ℒ⁡(𝜽,𝐪^n(B)).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}(\boldsymbol{\theta};B)\;\triangleq\;\mathcal{L}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\theta};\mathbf{Q}^{(B)}\bigr)\;=\;\frac{1}{500}\sum_{n=1}^{500}\mathcal{L}\bigl(\boldsymbol{\theta};\hat{\mathbf{q}}_{n}^{(B)}\bigr). (34)

We treat 𝐐(B)\mathbf{Q}^{(B)} directly as the weight vector 𝐪\mathbf{q} in Condition 1, so the corpus-level quantities ρt\rho_{t} and κ^(B)\hat{\kappa}^{(B)} defined below are instantiations of Condition 1 at 𝐐(B)\mathbf{Q}^{(B)}.

SFT training. For each budget B∈{1,3,5,10,20}B\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}, we run mini-batch SFT on ℒtotal​(⋅,B)\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}(\cdot;B) starting from 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}}, using the same hyperparameters as the main experiments. Full training details are deferred to Appendix C.3.

Recorded quantities. At each training step t∈{0,1,…,Tmax}t\in\{0,1,\ldots,T_{\max}\}, we record the corpus-level decay rate

ρt≜‖∇𝜽ℒtotal​(𝜽t,B)‖2ℒtotal​(𝜽t,B),\rho_{t}\;\triangleq\;\frac{\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t};B)\|^{2}}{\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t};B)}, (35)

and the anchor-relative ratio κ^t≜ρt/ρ0\hat{\kappa}_{t}\triangleq\rho_{t}/\rho_{0}, which is the discrete-time analog of ρ⁡(ϕ𝐐(B)​(s),𝐐(B))/ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐐(B))\rho(\phi_{\mathbf{Q}^{(B)}}(s);\mathbf{Q}^{(B)})/\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{Q}^{(B)}) in Condition 1. After training, for each BB we report the trajectory-wise minimum

κ^(B)≜mint∈[0,Tmax]⁡ρt/ρ0,\hat{\kappa}^{(B)}\;\triangleq\;\min_{t\in[0,T_{\max}]}\rho_{t}/\rho_{0}, (36)

as the empirical estimate of κ\kappa in Condition 1 under budget BB.

Findings.

Figure 5 reports the verification results for B∈{1,3,5,10,20}B\in\{1,3,5,10,20\}. Each panel plots the corpus-level decay rate ρt\rho_{t} (blue solid, left axis) and the anchor-relative ratio κ^t=ρt/ρ0\hat{\kappa}_{t}=\rho_{t}/\rho_{0} (red dashed, right axis) against the training step tt. The trajectory-wise minimum κ^(B)\hat{\kappa}^{(B)} and the step at which it is attained are annotated in each panel title.

We highlight three observations from the results.

  • •

    Condition 1 holds across all configurations. For every BB, the trajectory-wise minimum κ^(B)\hat{\kappa}^{(B)} is strictly positive (κ^(B)∈[0.012,0.279]\hat{\kappa}^{(B)}\in[0.012,0.279]), confirming that ρ\rho along the SFT trajectory does not collapse to zero relative to its anchor-time value. This empirically validates the existence of a positive κ\kappa in Condition 1.

  • •

    Smallest budget yields the largest κ^\hat{\kappa}. The minimum ratio at B=1B=1 (κ^(1)=0.279\hat{\kappa}^{(1)}=0.279) substantially exceeds the values for B≥3B\geq 3 (which fall in the range 0.0120.012–0.0150.015). Single-trajectory training produces a more stable ρ\rho trajectory and a tighter anchor-relative bound, while multi-trajectory training induces more oscillatory ρt\rho_{t} but still maintains a positive lower bound.

  • •

    κ^(B)\hat{\kappa}^{(B)} stabilizes for moderate BB. For B∈{3,5,10,20}B\in\{3,5,10,20\}, the minimum ratio remains within a narrow range (0.0120.012–0.0150.015), indicating that beyond a small budget, the corpus-level anchor-relative bound depends only weakly on BB.

On the early-step transient in ρt\rho_{t}.

A closer look at Figure 5 reveals that, for B≥3B\geq 3, ρt\rho_{t} is non-monotone: it exhibits a sharp transient spike during the first ∼\sim10% of training steps (reaching values an order of magnitude above ρ0\rho_{0}) before settling to a positive plateau. Two factors are consistent with this behavior. First, the empirical NTK Θ⁡(𝜽t,𝐪)\Theta(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t};\mathbf{q}) adapts most rapidly during the warmup phase of SFT, before the lazy-training regime of Assumption A.1 fully takes effect; the looser NTK stability in this early window admits larger fluctuations of ρt\rho_{t} around its anchor-time value. Second, weighted multi-trajectory gradients ∇𝜽ℒ​(𝜽t,𝐪)\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{t};\mathbf{q}) admit cancellation across trajectory blocks with different residual directions, which can produce non-monotone ‖∇𝜽ℒ‖2\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\mathcal{L}\|^{2} in early steps. Crucially, the empirical κ^(B)\hat{\kappa}^{(B)} reported in the panel titles is the trajectory-wise minimum of ρt/ρ0\rho_{t}/\rho_{0} over the entire training run, which already absorbs this transient: even at the lowest point of the trajectory, ρt/ρ0\rho_{t}/\rho_{0} remains bounded away from zero, which is exactly what Condition 1 requires. The transient therefore tightens (rather than relaxes) the empirical estimate of κ\kappa.

Appendix B Theoretical Analysis of LARK

This appendix collects the formal statements, proofs, and supporting derivations for the theoretical claims in Section 4.2 (the local linearization analysis of LARK) and Section 4.3 (the closed-form selection rule).

We begin in Appendix B.1 by establishing that ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q}) is quasiconvex on ΔK\Delta^{K} and that its (constrained or unconstrained) maximum collapses to a one-hot solution; this is the formal justification for the local-linearization strategy adopted in Section 4.2. Appendix B.2 fixes the additional notation and structural assumptions used by the rest of the appendix. Appendix B.3 collects auxiliary lemmas (gradient identities and bounds at the LM-head and backbone, together with the Taylor decomposition of ρ\rho around 𝐩\mathbf{p}) that are reused by the subsequent proofs. Appendices B.4, B.5, B.6, and B.7 respectively give the formal versions and full proofs of Lemma 1 (forward-pass ρk∗\rho_{k}^{*} estimation), Lemma 2 (χ2\chi^{2} controls both R1R_{1} and R2R_{2}), Theorem 1 (the LARK objective lower bound), and Lemma 3 (the BB-parameterized closed form). Finally, Appendix B.8 provides a quantitative error bound on the surrogate g^k\hat{g}_{k} relative to the exact directional derivative gk∗g_{k}^{*}, together with empirical evidence that the two are tightly correlated on real student models.

B.1 Quasiconvexity of ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q}) and Collapse to One-Hot

Throughout this subsection, fix 𝜽=𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}=\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}} and recall from Section 4.2 that 𝐠k=∇𝜽ℓk\mathbf{g}_{k}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell_{k} with ℓk=ℓ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐲k)>0\ell_{k}=\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}},\mathbf{y}_{k})>0. Define

N⁡(𝐪)≜‖∑kqk​𝐠k‖2=𝐪⊤​G​𝐪,D⁡(𝐪)≜∑kqk​ℓk,N(\mathbf{q})\;\triangleq\;\Bigl\|\textstyle\sum_{k}q_{k}\mathbf{g}_{k}\Bigr\|^{2}\;=\;\mathbf{q}^{\top}G\,\mathbf{q},\qquad D(\mathbf{q})\;\triangleq\;\textstyle\sum_{k}q_{k}\ell_{k}, (37)

where G∈ℝK×KG\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K} with Gi​j=⟨𝐠i,𝐠j⟩G_{ij}=\langle\mathbf{g}_{i},\,\mathbf{g}_{j}\rangle is the gradient Gram matrix. Since G⪰0G\succeq 0, N⁡(𝐪)N(\mathbf{q}) is a convex quadratic in 𝐪\mathbf{q}, and D⁡(𝐪)>0D(\mathbf{q})>0 is affine, so ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)=N⁡(𝐪)/D⁡(𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})=N(\mathbf{q})/D(\mathbf{q}).

Proposition 3 (Quasiconvexity of ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})).

ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q}) is quasiconvex in 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}.

Proof.

It suffices to show that for every c≥0c\geq 0, the sublevel set 𝒮c≜{𝐪∈ΔK:ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)≤c}\mathcal{S}_{c}\triangleq\{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}:\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})\leq c\} is convex. We have

𝐪∈𝒮c\displaystyle\mathbf{q}\in\mathcal{S}_{c} ⇔(a)ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)≤c\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{\iff}}\;\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})\leq c
⇔(b)N⁡(𝐪)D⁡(𝐪)≤c\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{\iff}}\;\frac{N(\mathbf{q})}{D(\mathbf{q})}\leq c
⇔(c)N⁡(𝐪)≤c⋅D⁡(𝐪)\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(c)}}{{\iff}}\;N(\mathbf{q})\leq c\cdot D(\mathbf{q})
⇔(d)𝐪⊤​G​𝐪−c​∑kqk​ℓk≤0,\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{\iff}}\;\mathbf{q}^{\top}G\,\mathbf{q}-c\textstyle\sum_{k}q_{k}\ell_{k}\leq 0, (38)

where (a) is the definition of 𝒮c\mathcal{S}_{c}; (b) substitutes ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)=N⁡(𝐪)/D⁡(𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})=N(\mathbf{q})/D(\mathbf{q}); (c) multiplies both sides by D⁡(𝐪)>0D(\mathbf{q})>0; and (d) substitutes the definitions of NN and DD from (37). The left-hand side of the final inequality in (38) is the sum of the convex quadratic 𝐪⊤​G​𝐪\mathbf{q}^{\top}G\,\mathbf{q} (since G⪰0G\succeq 0) and the affine term −c∑kqkℓk-c\sum_{k}q_{k}\ell_{k}, hence convex in 𝐪\mathbf{q}. Therefore 𝒮c\mathcal{S}_{c} is the intersection of a convex sublevel set with the convex set ΔK\Delta^{K}, which is convex. ∎

Corollary 1 (Maximum at a vertex).

max𝐪∈ΔK⁡ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\max_{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q}) is attained at an extreme point of ΔK\Delta^{K}.

Proof.

We have

max𝐪∈ΔK⁡ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\displaystyle\max_{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q}) =(a)max𝐪∈ΔK⁡ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)|extreme point\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{=}}\;\max_{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})\big|_{\text{extreme point}}
=(b)maxk∈[K]⁡ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐞k),\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{=}}\;\max_{k\in[K]}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{e}_{k}), (39)

where (a) follows because every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K} can be written as a convex combination of the extreme points {𝐞1,…,𝐞K}\{\mathbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{e}_{K}\}, namely 𝐪=∑k=1Kqk​𝐞k\mathbf{q}=\sum_{k=1}^{K}q_{k}\mathbf{e}_{k}, and quasiconvexity implies ρ(𝜽ref;𝐪)≤maxk∈[K]:qk>0ρ(𝜽ref;𝐞k)≤maxk∈[K]ρ(𝜽ref;𝐞k).\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})\leq\max_{k\in[K]:\,q_{k}>0}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{e}_{k})\leq\max_{k\in[K]}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{e}_{k}). The reverse inequality is immediate since each 𝐞k∈ΔK\mathbf{e}_{k}\in\Delta^{K}. Hence the maximum over ΔK\Delta^{K} is attained at an extreme point. Step (b) identifies the extreme points of ΔK\Delta^{K} as the standard basis vectors {𝐞1,…,𝐞K}\{\mathbf{e}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{e}_{K}\}. ∎

Corollary 2 (One-hot optimum).
max𝐪∈ΔK⁡ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)=maxk∈[K]⁡ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐞k)=maxk∈[K]⁡‖𝐠k‖2ℓk=maxk∈[K]⁡ρk∗.\max_{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})\;=\;\max_{k\in[K]}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{e}_{k})\;=\;\max_{k\in[K]}\frac{\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}}{\ell_{k}}\;=\;\max_{k\in[K]}\rho_{k}^{*}. (40)
Proof.

We have

max𝐪∈ΔK⁡ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\displaystyle\max_{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q}) =(a)maxk∈[K]⁡ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐞k)\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{=}}\;\max_{k\in[K]}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{e}_{k})
=(b)maxk∈[K]⁡N⁡(𝐞k)D⁡(𝐞k)=maxk∈[K]⁡‖𝐠k‖2ℓk=(c)maxk∈[K]⁡ρk∗,\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{=}}\;\max_{k\in[K]}\frac{N(\mathbf{e}_{k})}{D(\mathbf{e}_{k})}\;=\;\max_{k\in[K]}\frac{\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}}{\ell_{k}}\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(c)}}{{=}}\;\max_{k\in[K]}\rho_{k}^{*}, (41)

where (a) applies Corollary 1; (b) substitutes 𝐪=𝐞k\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{e}_{k} into the definitions in (37), giving N⁡(𝐞k)=‖𝐠k‖2N(\mathbf{e}_{k})=\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2} and D⁡(𝐞k)=ℓkD(\mathbf{e}_{k})=\ell_{k}; and (c) uses the definition ρk∗=‖𝐠k‖2/ℓk\rho_{k}^{*}=\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}/\ell_{k} from Section 4.2. ∎

B.2 Notation and Structural Assumptions

This subsection fixes the additional notation and structural assumptions used throughout Appendices B.3–B.8.

B.2.1 Notation

Symbols inherited from the main text.

We use the same symbols as Section 4.2: 𝐱\mathbf{x} is the question; 𝐲k=(y1k,…,y|ak|k)\mathbf{y}_{k}=(y_{1}^{k},\ldots,y_{|a_{k}|}^{k}) is the kk-th candidate trajectory, of length |ak||a_{k}|; 𝝅tk∈Δ|𝒱|\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}\in\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|} is the predictive distribution of the reference student πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} at position tt under teacher forcing; 𝜹⁡(ytk)∈Δ|𝒱|\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k})\in\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|} is the one-hot vector for the ground-truth token; ℓk=ℓ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐲k)\ell_{k}=\ell(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}},\mathbf{y}_{k}) is the length-normalized cross-entropy of trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k}; 𝐠k=∇𝜽ℓk\mathbf{g}_{k}=\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\ell_{k} is its gradient; ρk∗=‖𝐠k‖2/ℓk\rho_{k}^{*}=\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}/\ell_{k} is the per-trajectory rate; ρ^k\hat{\rho}_{k} is its forward-pass proxy (see Lemma 1); g^k\hat{g}_{k} and gk∗g_{k}^{*} are the surrogate and exact directional derivatives at 𝐩\mathbf{p}; R1,R2R_{1},R_{2} are the residual terms in (4); 𝐩=(1/K,…,1/K)∈ΔK\mathbf{p}=(1/K,\ldots,1/K)\in\Delta^{K} is the uniform prior.

Parameter decomposition.

We split the student parameters as 𝜽=(𝐖out,𝜽rest)\boldsymbol{\theta}=(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{rest}}), where 𝐖out∈ℝ|𝒱|×d\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d} is the LM head matrix and 𝜽rest\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{rest}} collects all backbone parameters. For each trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k} and position tt, the backbone produces a hidden state 𝐡t∈ℝd\mathbf{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the LM head produces logits 𝐳t=𝐖out​𝐡t∈ℝ|𝒱|\mathbf{z}_{t}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\mathbf{h}_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}, and 𝝅tk=softmax⁡(𝐳t)\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{t}). The token-level loss is ℓt=−log⁡πtk​(ytk)\ell_{t}=-\log\pi_{t}^{k}(y_{t}^{k}), so that ℓk=1|ak|​∑tℓt\ell_{k}=\tfrac{1}{|a_{k}|}\sum_{t}\ell_{t}.

Token-level residual.

We write the per-token prediction residual as 𝜹t≜𝝅tk−𝜹⁡(ytk)∈ℝ|𝒱|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}\triangleq\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}-\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k})\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}, which coincides with ∇𝐳tℓt\nabla_{\mathbf{z}_{t}}\ell_{t} by the standard softmax–cross-entropy identity (see Lemma 5 below).

Stacked matrices.

For each trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k} we collect the per-token residuals and hidden states into matrices

𝚫≜[𝜹1,…,𝜹|ak|]⊤∈ℝ|ak|×|𝒱|,𝐇≜[𝐡1,…,𝐡|ak|]⊤∈ℝ|ak|×d.\boldsymbol{\Delta}\;\triangleq\;[\boldsymbol{\delta}_{1},\ldots,\boldsymbol{\delta}_{|a_{k}|}]^{\top}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{|a_{k}|\times|\mathcal{V}|},\qquad\mathbf{H}\;\triangleq\;[\mathbf{h}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{h}_{|a_{k}|}]^{\top}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{|a_{k}|\times d}. (42)

We also write 𝐉H​(𝐲k)≜[∂𝐡t/∂𝜽rest]t=1|ak|∈ℝ|ak|​d×|𝜽rest|\mathbf{J}_{H}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\triangleq[\partial\mathbf{h}_{t}/\partial\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{rest}}]_{t=1}^{|a_{k}|}\in\mathbb{R}^{|a_{k}|\,d\times|\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{rest}}|} for the sequence-level Jacobian of the hidden states with respect to the backbone parameters. The dependence on 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k} is suppressed when the trajectory is clear from context.

Aggregated quantities.

Two aggregations of the per-token residual norms appear repeatedly. Define the (length-normalized) Brier score

Brier⁡(𝐲k)≜1|ak|​∑t=1|ak|‖𝜹t‖2=‖𝚫‖F2|ak|.\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\;\triangleq\;\tfrac{1}{|a_{k}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|a_{k}|}\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}\|^{2}\;=\;\tfrac{\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}}{|a_{k}|}. (43)

With this notation, the forward-pass proxy of Lemma 1 can be written as

ρ^k=∑t‖𝜹t‖2∑tℓt=Brier⁡(𝐲k)ℓk,\hat{\rho}_{k}\;=\;\frac{\sum_{t}\|\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}\|^{2}}{\sum_{t}\ell_{t}}\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k})}{\ell_{k}}, (44)

so that the 1/|ak|1/|a_{k}| factors cancel exactly in numerator and denominator.

Multi-trajectory quantities.

Across the candidate pool, write G∈ℝK×KG\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times K} for the gradient Gram matrix with Gi​j=⟨𝐠i,𝐠j⟩G_{ij}=\langle\mathbf{g}_{i},\mathbf{g}_{j}\rangle, and let ℓ=(ℓ1,…,ℓK)⊤\boldsymbol{\ell}=(\ell_{1},\ldots,\ell_{K})^{\top}. We use the shorthands

𝐠¯≜1K​∑k𝐠k,ℓ¯≜1K​∑kℓk,\bar{\mathbf{g}}\;\triangleq\;\tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_{k}\mathbf{g}_{k},\qquad\bar{\ell}\;\triangleq\;\tfrac{1}{K}\textstyle\sum_{k}\ell_{k}, (45)

together with ρ^max≜maxi⁡ρ^i\hat{\rho}_{\max}\triangleq\max_{i}\hat{\rho}_{i}, ℓmin≜mini⁡ℓi\ell_{\min}\triangleq\min_{i}\ell_{i}, and ℓmax≜maxi⁡ℓi\ell_{\max}\triangleq\max_{i}\ell_{i}. We also write ‖𝐯‖𝐩2≜∑kpk​vk2\|\mathbf{v}\|_{\mathbf{p}}^{2}\triangleq\sum_{k}p_{k}v_{k}^{2} for the 𝐩\mathbf{p}-weighted Euclidean norm; under uniform 𝐩\mathbf{p}, ‖𝐯‖𝐩2=1K​∑kvk2\|\mathbf{v}\|_{\mathbf{p}}^{2}=\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_{k}v_{k}^{2}.

B.2.2 Structural assumptions

We make four structural assumptions on the reference student πref\pi_{\mathrm{ref}} and its candidate-pool statistics. All four are mild conditions that are either standard in the convergence analysis of deep networks or directly verifiable from a single forward pass.

Assumption B.1 (Hidden-state norm stability).

There exist constants 0<C−≤C+0<C_{-}\leq C_{+} such that for every candidate trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k} and every token position tt,

C−2≤‖𝐡t‖2≤C+2.C_{-}^{2}\;\leq\;\|\mathbf{h}_{t}\|^{2}\;\leq\;C_{+}^{2}. (46)
Remark 3.

This holds naturally in modern LLMs employing RMSNorm [Zhang and Sennrich, 2019], which constrains hidden-state norms to a tight interval; we have C+/C−≈1C_{+}/C_{-}\approx 1 in practice.

Assumption B.2 (Local Jacobian conditioning).

There exists Λ>0\Lambda>0 such that for every candidate trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k},

λmax​(𝐉H​(𝐲k)​𝐉H​(𝐲k)⊤)≤Λ.\lambda_{\max}\bigl(\mathbf{J}_{H}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\,\mathbf{J}_{H}(\mathbf{y}_{k})^{\top}\bigr)\;\leq\;\Lambda. (47)
Remark 4.

This is a standard local Lipschitz continuity assumption on the backbone, widely adopted in convergence analyses of SFT [Liu et al., 2022].

Assumption B.3 (Matrix cosine alignment).

There exists ζ−>0\zeta_{-}>0 such that for every candidate trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k},

ζ⁡(𝐲k)≜‖𝚫⊤​𝐇‖F2‖𝚫‖F2⋅‖𝐇‖F2≥ζ−> 0.\zeta(\mathbf{y}_{k})\;\triangleq\;\frac{\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}}{\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}}\;\geq\;\zeta_{-}\;>\;0. (48)
Remark 5.

ζ⁡(𝐲k)\zeta(\mathbf{y}_{k}) is the squared Frobenius cosine similarity between the residual matrix 𝚫\boldsymbol{\Delta} and the hidden-state matrix 𝐇\mathbf{H}. Assumption B.3 requires that the joint signal between prediction residuals and hidden states does not degenerate, and is verifiable from a single forward pass.

Assumption B.4 (Strictly positive trajectory loss).

ℓmin=mini∈[K]⁡ℓi>0\ell_{\min}=\min_{i\in[K]}\ell_{i}>0.

Remark 6.

Under finite logits, ℓt>0\ell_{t}>0 at every token, so ℓk>0\ell_{k}>0 for every trajectory and Assumption B.4 holds automatically. We state it explicitly because it is needed in Appendix B.5 to ensure the Hessian of ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q}) is uniformly bounded over ΔK\Delta^{K} via D⁡(𝐪)=ℓ⊤​𝐪≥ℓminD(\mathbf{q})=\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\top}\mathbf{q}\geq\ell_{\min}.

B.3 Auxiliary Lemmas

This subsection collects building-block lemmas that are reused by the proofs in Appendices B.4–B.6. Lemmas 5–7 are the gradient identity and gradient norm bounds for the LM head and the backbone; they are the main tools for the proof of Lemma 1 in Appendix B.4. Lemma 8 gives the Taylor decomposition of ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q}) around the uniform prior 𝐩\mathbf{p}, together with the closed form of gk∗g_{k}^{*} and the definition of g^k\hat{g}_{k} in terms of forward-pass quantities; this is the starting identity for the proof of Lemma 2 in Appendix B.5. Lemma 9 provides a forward-computable upper bound on the entries of the gradient Gram matrix GG via the proxy ρ^i\hat{\rho}_{i}, which controls every GG-dependent quantity that appears in the proof of Lemma 2. Finally, Lemma 10 gives the closed-form Hessian of ρ\rho on ΔK\Delta^{K}, used to bound the second-order remainder R2R_{2}.

B.3.1 LM head and backbone gradient identities and bounds

Lemma 5 (LM head gradient).

Let ℓt=−log⁡πtk​(ytk)\ell_{t}=-\log\pi_{t}^{k}(y_{t}^{k}), 𝛑tk=softmax⁡(𝐳t)\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}=\mathrm{softmax}(\mathbf{z}_{t}), and 𝐳t=𝐖out​𝐡t\mathbf{z}_{t}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\mathbf{h}_{t}. Then

∂ℓt∂𝐖out=𝜹t​𝐡t⊤∈ℝ|𝒱|×d,∂ℓt∂𝐡t=𝐖out⊤​𝜹t.\frac{\partial\ell_{t}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}}\;=\;\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}\,\mathbf{h}_{t}^{\top}\;\in\;\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d},\qquad\frac{\partial\ell_{t}}{\partial\mathbf{h}_{t}}\;=\;\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}^{\top}\,\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}. (49)
Proof.

We prove the first identity; the second is immediate from the chain rule applied to 𝐳t=𝐖out​𝐡t\mathbf{z}_{t}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\mathbf{h}_{t}. For any direction 𝐔∈ℝ|𝒱|×d\mathbf{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|\times d},

⟨∂ℓt∂𝐖out,𝐔⟩F\displaystyle\left\langle\frac{\partial\ell_{t}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}},\,\mathbf{U}\right\rangle_{F} =(a)⟨∂ℓt∂𝐳t,∂𝐳t∂𝐖out​[𝐔]⟩\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{=}}\;\left\langle\frac{\partial\ell_{t}}{\partial\mathbf{z}_{t}},\,\frac{\partial\mathbf{z}_{t}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}}[\mathbf{U}]\right\rangle
=(b)⟨∂ℓt∂𝐳t,𝐔𝐡t⟩\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{=}}\;\left\langle\frac{\partial\ell_{t}}{\partial\mathbf{z}_{t}},\,\mathbf{U}\mathbf{h}_{t}\right\rangle
=(c)∑v=1|𝒱|∂ℓt∂zt,v​[𝐔𝐡t]v\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(c)}}{{=}}\;\sum_{v=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}\frac{\partial\ell_{t}}{\partial z_{t,v}}\,[\mathbf{U}\mathbf{h}_{t}]_{v}
=(d)∑v=1|𝒱|(πtk(v)−𝟏[v=ytk])[𝐔𝐡t]v\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\;\sum_{v=1}^{|\mathcal{V}|}\bigl(\pi_{t}^{k}(v)-\mathbf{1}[v=y_{t}^{k}]\bigr)\,[\mathbf{U}\mathbf{h}_{t}]_{v}
=(e)⟨𝝅tk−𝜹⁡(ytk),𝐔𝐡t⟩\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(e)}}{{=}}\;\langle\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}-\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k}),\,\mathbf{U}\mathbf{h}_{t}\rangle
=(f)⟨𝜹t​𝐡t⊤,𝐔⟩F,\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(f)}}{{=}}\;\langle\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}\,\mathbf{h}_{t}^{\top},\,\mathbf{U}\rangle_{F}, (50)

where (a) is the chain rule for the Fréchet derivative; (b) follows from the linearity of 𝐳t=𝐖out​𝐡t\mathbf{z}_{t}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\mathbf{h}_{t} in 𝐖out\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}, giving ∂𝐳t∂𝐖out​[𝐔]=𝐔𝐡t\frac{\partial\mathbf{z}_{t}}{\partial\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}}[\mathbf{U}]=\mathbf{U}\mathbf{h}_{t}; (c) expands the inner product componentwise; (d) is the standard softmax–cross-entropy gradient identity, ∂ℓt/∂zt,v=πtk(v)−𝟏[v=ytk]\partial\ell_{t}/\partial z_{t,v}=\pi_{t}^{k}(v)-\mathbf{1}[v=y_{t}^{k}], obtained by applying the quotient rule to πtk​(ytk)=ezt,ytk/∑v′ezt,v′\pi_{t}^{k}(y_{t}^{k})=e^{z_{t,y_{t}^{k}}}/\sum_{v^{\prime}}e^{z_{t,v^{\prime}}}; (e) recognizes the sum as ⟨𝜹t,𝐔𝐡t⟩\langle\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t},\mathbf{U}\mathbf{h}_{t}\rangle with 𝜹t=𝝅tk−𝜹⁡(ytk)\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}=\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}-\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k}); and (f) uses the trace identity ⟨𝐚,𝐁𝐜⟩=⟨𝐚𝐜⊤,𝐁⟩F\langle\mathbf{a},\mathbf{B}\mathbf{c}\rangle=\langle\mathbf{a}\mathbf{c}^{\top},\mathbf{B}\rangle_{F}. Since 𝐔\mathbf{U} was arbitrary, ∂ℓt/∂𝐖out=𝜹t​𝐡t⊤\partial\ell_{t}/\partial\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}=\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{\top}. ∎

Lemma 6 (LM head gradient bounds).

Under Assumptions B.1 and B.3, for every candidate trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k},

ζ−​C−2​Brier​(𝐲k)≤‖∇𝐖outℓk‖F2≤C+2​Brier​(𝐲k).\zeta_{-}\,C_{-}^{2}\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\;\leq\;\|\nabla_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}}\ell_{k}\|_{F}^{2}\;\leq\;C_{+}^{2}\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k}). (51)
Proof.

By Lemma 5 and the definition ℓk=1|ak|​∑tℓt\ell_{k}=\tfrac{1}{|a_{k}|}\sum_{t}\ell_{t},

∇𝐖outℓk=1|ak|​∑t𝜹t​𝐡t⊤=1|ak|​𝚫⊤​𝐇,\nabla_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}}\ell_{k}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{|a_{k}|}\textstyle\sum_{t}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}\mathbf{h}_{t}^{\top}\;=\;\tfrac{1}{|a_{k}|}\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}, (52)

where the second equality follows from the definitions of 𝚫,𝐇\boldsymbol{\Delta},\mathbf{H} in (42). Hence ‖∇𝐖outℓk‖F2=‖𝚫⊤​𝐇‖F2/|ak|2\|\nabla_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}}\ell_{k}\|_{F}^{2}=\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}/|a_{k}|^{2}.

Lower bound.

‖∇𝐖outℓk‖F2\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}}\ell_{k}\|_{F}^{2} =(a)‖𝚫⊤​𝐇‖F2|ak|2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{=}}\;\frac{\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}}{|a_{k}|^{2}}
≥(b)ζ−​‖𝚫‖F2​‖𝐇‖F2|ak|2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{\geq}}\;\frac{\zeta_{-}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}\,\|\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}}{|a_{k}|^{2}}
≥(c)ζ−​|ak|​Brier​(𝐲k)⋅|ak|​C−2|ak|2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(c)}}{{\geq}}\;\frac{\zeta_{-}\,|a_{k}|\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\cdot|a_{k}|\,C_{-}^{2}}{|a_{k}|^{2}}
=ζ−​C−2​Brier​(𝐲k),\displaystyle\;=\;\zeta_{-}\,C_{-}^{2}\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k}), (53)

where (a) is (52); (b) applies Assumption B.3, which gives ‖𝚫⊤​𝐇‖F2≥ζ−​‖𝚫‖F2​‖𝐇‖F2\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}\geq\zeta_{-}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}\,\|\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}; and (c) substitutes ‖𝚫‖F2=|ak|​Brier​(𝐲k)\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}=|a_{k}|\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k}) from (43) together with ‖𝐇‖F2=∑t‖𝐡t‖2≥|ak|​C−2\|\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{t}\|\mathbf{h}_{t}\|^{2}\geq|a_{k}|\,C_{-}^{2} from Assumption B.1.

Upper bound.

‖∇𝐖outℓk‖F2\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}}\ell_{k}\|_{F}^{2} =(d)‖𝚫⊤​𝐇‖F2|ak|2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\;\frac{\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}}{|a_{k}|^{2}}
≤(e)‖𝚫‖F2​‖𝐇‖F2|ak|2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(e)}}{{\leq}}\;\frac{\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}\,\|\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}}{|a_{k}|^{2}}
≤(f)|ak|​Brier​(𝐲k)⋅|ak|​C+2|ak|2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(f)}}{{\leq}}\;\frac{|a_{k}|\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\cdot|a_{k}|\,C_{+}^{2}}{|a_{k}|^{2}}
=C+2​Brier​(𝐲k),\displaystyle\;=\;C_{+}^{2}\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k}), (54)

where (d) is (52); (e) is the matrix Cauchy–Schwarz inequality ‖𝚫⊤​𝐇‖F2≤‖𝚫‖F2​‖𝐇‖F2\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}^{\top}\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}\leq\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}\,\|\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}; and (f) substitutes ‖𝚫‖F2=|ak|​Brier​(𝐲k)\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}=|a_{k}|\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k}) from (43) together with ‖𝐇‖F2=∑t‖𝐡t‖2≤|ak|​C+2\|\mathbf{H}\|_{F}^{2}=\sum_{t}\|\mathbf{h}_{t}\|^{2}\leq|a_{k}|\,C_{+}^{2} from Assumption B.1. ∎

Lemma 7 (Backbone gradient bound).

Under Assumptions B.1 and B.2, for every candidate trajectory 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k},

‖∇𝜽restℓk‖2≤Λ​‖𝐖out‖op2|ak|​Brier​(𝐲k).\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{rest}}}\ell_{k}\|^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{\Lambda\,\|\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}}{|a_{k}|}\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k}). (55)
Proof.

By the chain rule together with the second identity of Lemma 5, ∂ℓt/∂𝐡t=𝐖out⊤​𝜹t\partial\ell_{t}/\partial\mathbf{h}_{t}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{\delta}_{t}, hence

∇𝜽restℓk=𝐉H​(𝐲k)⊤​vec​(1|ak|​𝚫​𝐖out).\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{rest}}}\ell_{k}\;=\;\mathbf{J}_{H}(\mathbf{y}_{k})^{\top}\,\mathrm{vec}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{|a_{k}|}\boldsymbol{\Delta}\,\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\right). (56)

Then

‖∇𝜽restℓk‖2\displaystyle\|\nabla_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{rest}}}\ell_{k}\|^{2} ≤(a)λmax​(𝐉H​(𝐲k)​𝐉H​(𝐲k)⊤)​‖vec⁡(1|ak|​𝚫​𝐖out)‖2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{\leq}}\;\lambda_{\max}\bigl(\mathbf{J}_{H}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\,\mathbf{J}_{H}(\mathbf{y}_{k})^{\top}\bigr)\left\|\mathrm{vec}\!\left(\tfrac{1}{|a_{k}|}\boldsymbol{\Delta}\,\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\right)\right\|^{2}
≤(b)Λ|ak|2​‖𝚫​𝐖out‖F2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{\leq}}\;\frac{\Lambda}{|a_{k}|^{2}}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\,\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\|_{F}^{2}
≤(c)Λ​‖𝐖out‖op2|ak|2​‖𝚫‖F2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(c)}}{{\leq}}\;\frac{\Lambda\,\|\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}}{|a_{k}|^{2}}\,\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}
=(d)Λ​‖𝐖out‖op2|ak|​Brier​(𝐲k),\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\;\frac{\Lambda\,\|\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}}{|a_{k}|}\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k}), (57)

where (a) uses ‖𝐀⊤​𝐯‖2≤λmax​(𝐀𝐀⊤)​‖𝐯‖2\|\mathbf{A}^{\top}\mathbf{v}\|^{2}\leq\lambda_{\max}(\mathbf{A}\mathbf{A}^{\top})\|\mathbf{v}\|^{2} with 𝐀=𝐉H​(𝐲k)\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{J}_{H}(\mathbf{y}_{k}); (b) applies Assumption B.2 together with the identity ‖vec⁡(𝐌)‖2=‖𝐌‖F2\|\mathrm{vec}(\mathbf{M})\|^{2}=\|\mathbf{M}\|_{F}^{2}; (c) uses the submultiplicativity ‖𝚫​𝐖out‖F≤‖𝐖out‖op​‖𝚫‖F\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\,\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\|_{F}\leq\|\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}; and (d) substitutes ‖𝚫‖F2=|ak|​Brier​(𝐲k)\|\boldsymbol{\Delta}\|_{F}^{2}=|a_{k}|\,\mathrm{Brier}(\mathbf{y}_{k}) from (43). ∎

B.3.2 Taylor decomposition of ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})

The next lemma packages the algebraic preliminaries for the linearization argument: the closed form of the exact directional derivative gk∗g_{k}^{*}, the definition of the forward-pass surrogate g^k\hat{g}_{k}, and the resulting decomposition of the change in ρ\rho into a linear term plus two residuals.

Lemma 8 (Taylor decomposition).

Let N⁡(𝐪)≜‖∑kqk​𝐠k‖2=𝐪⊤​G​𝐪N(\mathbf{q})\triangleq\|\sum_{k}q_{k}\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}=\mathbf{q}^{\top}G\mathbf{q} and D⁡(𝐪)≜∑kqk​ℓk=ℓ⊤​𝐪D(\mathbf{q})\triangleq\sum_{k}q_{k}\ell_{k}=\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\top}\mathbf{q}, so that ρ⁡(𝛉ref,𝐪)=N⁡(𝐪)/D⁡(𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})=N(\mathbf{q})/D(\mathbf{q}). Then:

  • (i)

    (Closed form of gk∗g_{k}^{*}.) The exact directional derivative at 𝐩\mathbf{p} satisfies

    gk∗=∂∂qk​N⁡(𝐪)D⁡(𝐪)|𝐪=𝐩=2​𝐠k⊤​𝐠¯ℓ¯−ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)​ℓkℓ¯.g_{k}^{*}\;=\;\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{k}}\frac{N(\mathbf{q})}{D(\mathbf{q})}\right|_{\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p}}\;=\;\frac{2\,\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{g}}}{\bar{\ell}}\;-\;\frac{\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{p})\,\ell_{k}}{\bar{\ell}}. (58)
  • (ii)

    (Forward-pass surrogate.) Applying the diagonal approximations 𝐠k⊤​𝐠¯≈‖𝐠k‖2/K\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{g}}\approx\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}/K and ‖𝐠¯‖2≈1K2​∑i‖𝐠i‖2\|\bar{\mathbf{g}}\|^{2}\approx\tfrac{1}{K^{2}}\sum_{i}\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2} in (58), and substituting the proxy ρ^i\hat{\rho}_{i} for ρi∗=‖𝐠i‖2/ℓi\rho_{i}^{*}=\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2}/\ell_{i}, gives

    g^k=ℓk∑iℓi​(2​ρ^k−∑iρ^i​ℓi∑iℓi).\hat{g}_{k}\;=\;\frac{\ell_{k}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}\!\left(2\hat{\rho}_{k}-\frac{\sum_{i}\hat{\rho}_{i}\,\ell_{i}}{\sum_{i}\ell_{i}}\right). (59)
  • (iii)

    (Decomposition.) Setting 𝜼≜𝐠^−𝐠∗\boldsymbol{\eta}\triangleq\hat{\mathbf{g}}-\mathbf{g}^{*}, the change in ρ\rho admits the decomposition

    ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)−ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)=⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩+R1+R2,\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{p})\;=\;\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle\;+\;R_{1}\;+\;R_{2}, (60)

    where

    R1≜−⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝜼⟩,R2≜ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)−ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)−⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠∗⟩R_{1}\;\triangleq\;-\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\boldsymbol{\eta}\rangle,\qquad R_{2}\;\triangleq\;\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{p})-\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\mathbf{g}^{*}\rangle (61)

    are the surrogate substitution error and the second-order Taylor remainder, respectively.

Proof.

For (i), apply the quotient rule to N⁡(𝐪)/D⁡(𝐪)N(\mathbf{q})/D(\mathbf{q}):

∂∂qk​N⁡(𝐪)D⁡(𝐪)=D(𝐪)⋅2𝐠k⊤∑iqi𝐠i−N(𝐪)ℓkD​(𝐪)2.\frac{\partial}{\partial q_{k}}\frac{N(\mathbf{q})}{D(\mathbf{q})}\;=\;\frac{D(\mathbf{q})\cdot 2\,\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\!\sum_{i}q_{i}\mathbf{g}_{i}-N(\mathbf{q})\,\ell_{k}}{D(\mathbf{q})^{2}}. (62)

Evaluating at 𝐪=𝐩\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p} with pk=1/Kp_{k}=1/K gives ∑ipi​𝐠i=𝐠¯\sum_{i}p_{i}\mathbf{g}_{i}=\bar{\mathbf{g}}, D⁡(𝐩)=ℓ¯D(\mathbf{p})=\bar{\ell}, and N⁡(𝐩)/D⁡(𝐩)=ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)N(\mathbf{p})/D(\mathbf{p})=\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{p}), yielding (58).

For (ii), substitute 𝐠k⊤​𝐠¯≈‖𝐠k‖2/K\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{g}}\approx\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}/K and ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)=‖𝐠¯‖2/ℓ¯≈1K2​ℓ¯​∑i‖𝐠i‖2\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{p})=\|\bar{\mathbf{g}}\|^{2}/\bar{\ell}\approx\tfrac{1}{K^{2}\bar{\ell}}\sum_{i}\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2} into (58), and replace each ‖𝐠i‖2=ρi∗​ℓi\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2}=\rho_{i}^{*}\,\ell_{i} by ρ^i​ℓi\hat{\rho}_{i}\,\ell_{i}. Using K​ℓ¯=∑iℓiK\bar{\ell}=\sum_{i}\ell_{i} and simplifying gives (59).

For (iii), expand ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)−ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)=⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠∗⟩+R2\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{p})=\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\mathbf{g}^{*}\rangle+R_{2} by definition of R2R_{2}, and add and subtract ⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle to obtain (60) with R1R_{1} as in (61). ∎

B.3.3 Forward-computable bound on the gradient Gram matrix

The next lemma upgrades the per-trajectory bound of Lemma 1 to a uniform, forward-computable bound on every entry of the gradient Gram matrix GG. It is the main tool that lets us replace gradient-dependent quantities (such as 𝐠k⊤​𝐠¯\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{g}}, ‖𝐠¯‖2\|\bar{\mathbf{g}}\|^{2}, and ‖G‖op\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}) by forward-only quantities throughout the proofs of Lemma 2 and Theorem 1.

Lemma 9 (Gram-matrix entry bound).

Assume Assumptions B.1–B.3, and let

E+≜C+2​maxi∈[K]⁡(1+εhead​(|ai|)),εhead​(|ai|)=Λ​‖𝐖out‖op2C+2​|ai|,E_{+}\;\triangleq\;C_{+}^{2}\max_{i\in[K]}\bigl(1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{head}}(|a_{i}|)\bigr),\qquad\varepsilon_{\mathrm{head}}(|a_{i}|)\;=\;\frac{\Lambda\,\|\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}}{C_{+}^{2}\,|a_{i}|}, (63)

so that Lemma 1 yields the uniform inequality ρi∗≤E+​ρ^i\rho_{i}^{*}\leq E_{+}\,\hat{\rho}_{i} for every i∈[K]i\in[K]. Then for every i,j∈[K]i,j\in[K],

|Gi​j|≤Gi​i​Gj​j=ρi∗​ρj∗​ℓi​ℓj≤E+​ρ^i​ρ^j​ℓi​ℓj.|G_{ij}|\;\leq\;\sqrt{G_{ii}\,G_{jj}}\;=\;\sqrt{\rho_{i}^{*}\,\rho_{j}^{*}\,\ell_{i}\,\ell_{j}}\;\leq\;E_{+}\sqrt{\hat{\rho}_{i}\,\hat{\rho}_{j}\,\ell_{i}\,\ell_{j}}. (64)
Proof.

We have

|Gi​j|\displaystyle|G_{ij}| ≤(a)Gi​i​Gj​j\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{\leq}}\;\sqrt{G_{ii}\,G_{jj}}
=(b)ρi∗​ρj∗​ℓi​ℓj\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{=}}\;\sqrt{\rho_{i}^{*}\,\rho_{j}^{*}\,\ell_{i}\,\ell_{j}}

where (a) is the entry-wise Cauchy–Schwarz bound for inner products, |⟨𝐠i,𝐠j⟩|≤‖𝐠i‖​‖𝐠j‖|\langle\mathbf{g}_{i},\mathbf{g}_{j}\rangle|\leq\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|\|\mathbf{g}_{j}\|; (b) uses Gi​i=‖𝐠i‖2=ρi∗​ℓiG_{ii}=\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2}=\rho_{i}^{*}\,\ell_{i} from the definition ρi∗=‖𝐠i‖2/ℓi\rho_{i}^{*}=\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2}/\ell_{i}; and (c) applies the upper part of Lemma 1 entry-wise to each of ρi∗\rho_{i}^{*} and ρj∗\rho_{j}^{*}. ∎

All bounds derived in Appendix B.5 (the proof of Lemma 2) trace back to (64). In particular, both the off-diagonal residuals appearing in the surrogate substitution error and the operator-norm bound on GG used in the Hessian analysis are obtained by summing (64) over the appropriate index sets.

B.3.4 Hessian of ρ\rho on the simplex

Lemma 10 (Hessian formula).

On the relative interior of ΔK\Delta^{K}, the Hessian of ρ⁡(𝛉ref,𝐪)=N⁡(𝐪)/D⁡(𝐪)\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})=N(\mathbf{q})/D(\mathbf{q}) in 𝐪\mathbf{q} is

∇𝐪2ρ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)=1D⁡(𝐪)​[ 2​G−ℓ​(∇ρ)⊤−(∇ρ)​ℓ⊤],\nabla^{2}_{\mathbf{q}}\,\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})\;=\;\frac{1}{D(\mathbf{q})}\Bigl[\,2\,G\;-\;\boldsymbol{\ell}\,(\nabla\rho)^{\top}\;-\;(\nabla\rho)\,\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\top}\,\Bigr], (66)

where ∇ρ=(2​G​𝐪−ρ​ℓ)/D⁡(𝐪)\nabla\rho=(2\,G\mathbf{q}-\rho\,\boldsymbol{\ell})/D(\mathbf{q}).

Proof.

The quotient rule applied to ρ=N/D\rho=N/D gives ∇ρ=(∇N−ρ∇D)/D=(2G𝐪−ρℓ)/D\nabla\rho=(\nabla N-\rho\,\nabla D)/D=(2\,G\mathbf{q}-\rho\,\boldsymbol{\ell})/D, or equivalently D∇ρ=2G𝐪−ρℓD\,\nabla\rho=2\,G\mathbf{q}-\rho\,\boldsymbol{\ell}. Differentiating both sides with respect to 𝐪\mathbf{q}, using ∇D=ℓ\nabla D=\boldsymbol{\ell} and the product rule ∇(D∇ρ)=ℓ(∇ρ)⊤+D∇2ρ\nabla(D\nabla\rho)=\boldsymbol{\ell}\,(\nabla\rho)^{\top}+D\,\nabla^{2}\rho, gives

ℓ​(∇ρ)⊤+D​∇2ρ= 2​G−(∇ρ)​ℓ⊤.\boldsymbol{\ell}\,(\nabla\rho)^{\top}+D\,\nabla^{2}\rho\;=\;2\,G\;-\;(\nabla\rho)\,\boldsymbol{\ell}^{\top}. (67)

Solving for ∇2ρ\nabla^{2}\rho and noting that the left-hand side is symmetric (which forces the symmetrized form of the rank-2 correction) yields (66). ∎
