‖∇ρ‖≤2​‖G‖op​‖𝐪‖+ρ​‖ℓ‖D⁡(𝐪)≤‖G‖opℓmin​(2+‖ℓ‖ℓmin).\|\nabla\rho\|\leq\frac{2\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}\|\mathbf{q}\|+\rho\|\boldsymbol{\ell}\|}{D(\mathbf{q})}\leq\frac{\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\ell_{\min}}\left(2+\frac{\|\boldsymbol{\ell}\|}{\ell_{\min}}\right). (104)

Substituting (104) into (102) and using D⁡(𝐪)≥ℓminD(\mathbf{q})\geq\ell_{\min} gives

‖∇𝐪2ρ‖op≤2​‖G‖opℓmin​(1+‖ℓ‖ℓmin)2.\|\nabla_{\mathbf{q}}^{2}\rho\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\frac{2\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}}{\ell_{\min}}\left(1+\frac{\|\boldsymbol{\ell}\|}{\ell_{\min}}\right)^{2}. (105)

By Lemma 9,

‖G‖op≤‖G‖F≤E+​∑i,jρ^i​ρ^j​ℓi​ℓj=E+​∑iρ^i​ℓi.\|G\|_{\mathrm{op}}\leq\|G\|_{F}\leq E_{+}\sqrt{\sum_{i,j}\hat{\rho}_{i}\hat{\rho}_{j}\ell_{i}\ell_{j}}=E_{+}\sum_{i}\hat{\rho}_{i}\ell_{i}. (106)

Together with ‖ℓ‖≤K​ℓmax\|\boldsymbol{\ell}\|\leq\sqrt{K}\,\ell_{\max}, this yields

M≤2​E+​∑iρ^i​ℓiℓmin​(1+K​ℓmaxℓmin)2.M\leq\frac{2E_{+}\sum_{i}\hat{\rho}_{i}\ell_{i}}{\ell_{\min}}\left(1+\frac{\sqrt{K}\,\ell_{\max}}{\ell_{\min}}\right)^{2}. (107)

Substituting (107) into (100) gives

|R2|≤α2χ2(𝐪∥𝐩),|R_{2}|\leq\alpha_{2}\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\,\|\,\mathbf{p}),

with α2\alpha_{2} as in (82). This proves the second bound in (80) and completes the proof. ∎

Remark 8 (Operational meaning of α1rms\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}}).

The quantity α1rms\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}} defined in (98) is a 𝐩\mathbf{p}-weighted RMS bound on the surrogate error:

1K​∑k=1K|g^k−gk∗|2=‖𝐠^−𝐠∗‖𝐩≤α1rms.\sqrt{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}|\hat{g}_{k}-g_{k}^{*}|^{2}}=\|\hat{\mathbf{g}}-\mathbf{g}^{*}\|_{\mathbf{p}}\leq\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}}. (108)

The constant α1=(α1rms)2/4\alpha_{1}=(\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}})^{2}/4 in (81) is the coefficient obtained after absorbing the square-root residual into the χ2\chi^{2} term through Young’s inequality. This is an aggregate bound rather than a per-coordinate one: in the worst case, an individual error |g^k−gk∗||\hat{g}_{k}-g_{k}^{*}| can be as large as K​α1rms\sqrt{K}\,\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}}. The use of the RMS norm is natural here because the Cauchy–Schwarz step in (83) pairs χ2(𝐪∥𝐩)\sqrt{\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\,\|\,\mathbf{p})} with ‖𝜼‖𝐩\|\boldsymbol{\eta}\|_{\mathbf{p}}.

B.6 Proof of Theorem 1 (LARK Objective)

This subsection states and proves the formal version of Theorem 1. The informal statement in the main text asserts the existence of finite constants α>0\alpha>0 and C∈ℝC\in\mathbb{R}, independent of the optimization variable 𝐪\mathbf{q}, realizing a χ2\chi^{2}-regularized lower bound on the learnability improvement; the formal version below makes both constants explicit in terms of the constants α1,α2\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2} from Lemma 12.

Theorem 2 (Formal version of Theorem 1).

Under Assumptions B.1–B.4, for every 𝐪∈ΔK\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K},

ρ(𝜽ref;𝐪)−ρ(𝜽ref;𝐩)≥⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩−αχ2(𝐪∥𝐩)+C,\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{p})\;\geq\;\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle\;-\;\alpha\,\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\,\|\,\mathbf{p})\;+\;C, (109)

where

α≜α1+α2> 0,C≜−1,\alpha\;\triangleq\;\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\;>\;0,\qquad C\;\triangleq\;-1, (110)

and α1,α2>0\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}>0 are the explicit constants given by Lemma 12. In particular, α\alpha and CC are independent of 𝐪\mathbf{q}.

Proof.

By Lemma 8(iii), the change in ρ\rho admits the exact decomposition

ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)−ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)=⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩+R1+R2.\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{p})\;=\;\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle\;+\;R_{1}\;+\;R_{2}. (111)

By Lemma 12, the two residuals satisfy

|R1|≤α1χ2(𝐪∥𝐩)+1,|R2|≤α2χ2(𝐪∥𝐩),|R_{1}|\;\leq\;\alpha_{1}\,\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\,\|\,\mathbf{p})+1,\qquad|R_{2}|\;\leq\;\alpha_{2}\,\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\,\|\,\mathbf{p}), (112)

where α1,α2>0\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2}>0 are given by (81) and (82), respectively. Combining (111) and (112) gives

ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)−ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐩)\displaystyle\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{q})-\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\,\mathbf{p}) =(a)⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩+R1+R2\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(a)}}{{=}}\;\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle\;+\;R_{1}\;+\;R_{2}
≥(b)⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩−|R1|−|R2|\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(b)}}{{\geq}}\;\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle\;-\;|R_{1}|\;-\;|R_{2}|
≥(c)⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩−(α1χ2(𝐪∥𝐩)+1)−α2χ2(𝐪∥𝐩)\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(c)}}{{\geq}}\;\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle\;-\;\bigl(\alpha_{1}\,\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\,\|\,\mathbf{p})+1\bigr)\;-\;\alpha_{2}\,\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\,\|\,\mathbf{p})
=(d)⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩−(α1+α2)χ2(𝐪∥𝐩)− 1,\displaystyle\;\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\;\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle\;-\;(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})\,\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\,\|\,\mathbf{p})\;-\;1, (113)

where (a) is (111); (b) uses R1,R2≥−|R1|,−|R2|R_{1},R_{2}\geq-|R_{1}|,-|R_{2}|; (c) substitutes the bounds (112) from Lemma 12; and (d) collects the two χ2\chi^{2} terms. Identifying α=α1+α2\alpha=\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2} and C=−1C=-1 as in (110) yields (109). ∎

Remark 9 (Correspondence with the informal constants α\alpha and CC).

Theorem 2 instantiates the informal constants α,C\alpha,C of Theorem 1 as α=α1+α2\alpha=\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2} and C=−1C=-1, where α1,α2\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2} are the forward-computable constants from Lemma 12. The resulting bound depends on 𝐪\mathbf{q} only through the linear term ⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle and the χ2\chi^{2} regularization. Since C=−1C=-1 is independent of 𝐪\mathbf{q}, it does not affect the maximizer of the right-hand side over ΔK\Delta^{K}. The coefficient α\alpha motivates the use of a χ2\chi^{2} penalty; in the fixed-budget selection rule of Section 4.3, the penalty temperature is calibrated as τ⁡(B)\tau(B) so that the optimizer has exactly BB active trajectories.

B.7 Proof of Lemma 3 (BB-Parameterized Closed Form)

Theorem 2 motivates a χ2\chi^{2}-regularized linear surrogate. In the fixed-budget setting, we calibrate the regularization temperature so that the optimizer has exactly BB active coordinates. By the equivalence (77) between the χ2\chi^{2}-divergence and the squared Euclidean distance under the uniform prior, the corresponding objective can be written as

𝐪^=arg⁡max𝐪∈ΔK​{⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩−τ​K2​‖𝐪−𝐩‖2},\hat{\mathbf{q}}\;=\;\arg\max_{\mathbf{q}\in\Delta^{K}}\bigg\{\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle\;-\;\frac{\tau\,K}{2}\,\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p}\|^{2}\bigg\}, (114)

where we write τ\tau for the temperature to be chosen as a function of the budget BB.

Proof of Lemma 3.

The objective (114) is strictly concave in 𝐪\mathbf{q} whenever τ​K>0\tau K>0, so the KKT conditions characterize its unique global maximizer over ΔK\Delta^{K}. Introduce a Lagrange multiplier λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R} for the equality constraint ∑kqk=1\sum_{k}q_{k}=1 and KKT multipliers μk≥0\mu_{k}\geq 0 for the non-negativity constraints qk≥0q_{k}\geq 0. The Lagrangian is

ℒ⁡(𝐪,λ,𝝁)=⟨𝐪−𝐩,𝐠^⟩−τ​K2​‖𝐪−𝐩‖2−λ⁡(∑kqk−1)+∑kμk​qk.\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{q},\lambda,\boldsymbol{\mu})=\langle\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p},\,\hat{\mathbf{g}}\rangle-\frac{\tau K}{2}\|\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{p}\|^{2}-\lambda\Bigl(\sum_{k}q_{k}-1\Bigr)+\sum_{k}\mu_{k}q_{k}. (115)

Stationarity and complementary slackness give

g^k−τ​K​(qk−pk)−λ+μk=0,μk​qk=0,μk≥0.\hat{g}_{k}-\tau K(q_{k}-p_{k})-\lambda+\mu_{k}=0,\qquad\mu_{k}q_{k}=0,\qquad\mu_{k}\geq 0. (116)

Since pk=1/Kp_{k}=1/K, these conditions imply the projection form

q^k=[1K+g^k−λτ​K]+,\hat{q}_{k}=\left[\frac{1}{K}+\frac{\hat{g}_{k}-\lambda}{\tau K}\right]_{+}, (117)

where [x]+=max⁡{x,0}[x]_{+}=\max\{x,0\}. The threshold λ\lambda is determined by the normalization condition ∑kq^k=1\sum_{k}\hat{q}_{k}=1.

Sort the scores as g^(1)≥g^(2)≥⋯≥g^(K)\hat{g}_{(1)}\geq\hat{g}_{(2)}\geq\cdots\geq\hat{g}_{(K)}, where (i)(i) denotes the sorted index. From (117), q^(i)>0\hat{q}_{(i)}>0 if and only if g^(i)>λ−τ\hat{g}_{(i)}>\lambda-\tau. Thus an active set of size BB is obtained whenever

g^(B)>λ−τ≥g^(B+1).\hat{g}_{(B)}>\lambda-\tau\geq\hat{g}_{(B+1)}. (118)

Under the assumption g^(B)>g^(B+1)\hat{g}_{(B)}>\hat{g}_{(B+1)}, the top-BB active set is well-defined. We choose the boundary value

λ=g^(B+1)+τ,\lambda=\hat{g}_{(B+1)}+\tau, (119)

which makes the (B+1)(B+1)-st coordinate exactly inactive while keeping the first BB coordinates positive.

Substituting (119) into (117), for every i≤Bi\leq B we obtain

q^(i)\displaystyle\hat{q}_{(i)} =1K+g^(i)−g^(B+1)−ττ​K\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K}+\frac{\hat{g}_{(i)}-\hat{g}_{(B+1)}-\tau}{\tau K}
=g^(i)−g^(B+1)τ​K.\displaystyle=\frac{\hat{g}_{(i)}-\hat{g}_{(B+1)}}{\tau K}. (120)

For i>Bi>B, the projection in (117) gives q^(i)=0\hat{q}_{(i)}=0. Imposing the simplex normalization on the active coordinates gives

1=∑i=1Bq^(i)=1τ​K​∑i=1B(g^(i)−g^(B+1)).1=\sum_{i=1}^{B}\hat{q}_{(i)}=\frac{1}{\tau K}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\bigl(\hat{g}_{(i)}-\hat{g}_{(B+1)}\bigr). (121)

Therefore the budget-calibrated temperature is

τ∗​(B)=1K​∑i=1B(g^(i)−g^(B+1)),\tau^{*}(B)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\bigl(\hat{g}_{(i)}-\hat{g}_{(B+1)}\bigr), (122)

which is positive because g^(B)>g^(B+1)\hat{g}_{(B)}>\hat{g}_{(B+1)}. Substituting (122) into (120) yields

q^(i)=g^(i)−g^(B+1)∑j=1B(g^(j)−g^(B+1))for ​i≤B,q^(i)=0for ​i>B.\hat{q}_{(i)}=\frac{\hat{g}_{(i)}-\hat{g}_{(B+1)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{B}\bigl(\hat{g}_{(j)}-\hat{g}_{(B+1)}\bigr)}\quad\text{for }i\leq B,\qquad\hat{q}_{(i)}=0\quad\text{for }i>B. (123)

This is the closed-form BB-parameterized weighting rule stated in Lemma 3. ∎

B.8 Theoretical and Empirical Validation of the Surrogate 𝐠^\hat{\mathbf{g}}

The forward-pass surrogate 𝐠^\hat{\mathbf{g}} is the central computational shortcut underlying the LARK algorithm: it replaces the exact directional derivative 𝐠∗=∇𝐪ρ​(𝜽ref,𝐪)|𝐪=𝐩\mathbf{g}^{*}=\nabla_{\mathbf{q}}\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})|_{\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p}}, whose evaluation requires one backward pass per candidate trajectory, with a quantity computable from forward passes alone. This subsection studies the relationship between 𝐠^\hat{\mathbf{g}} and 𝐠∗\mathbf{g}^{*} from two complementary perspectives: a theoretical RMS error bound and an empirical comparison on real student models.

B.8.1 Theoretical Error Bound

The bounds derived in Appendix B.5 immediately yield a quantitative bound on ‖𝐠^−𝐠∗‖\|\hat{\mathbf{g}}-\mathbf{g}^{*}\| in the 𝐩\mathbf{p}-weighted norm ‖𝐯‖𝐩2≜K−1​∑kvk2\|\mathbf{v}\|_{\mathbf{p}}^{2}\triangleq K^{-1}\sum_{k}v_{k}^{2}.

Corollary 3 (𝐩\mathbf{p}-weighted RMS error of 𝐠^\hat{\mathbf{g}}).

Under Assumptions B.1–B.4,

‖𝐠^−𝐠∗‖𝐩=1K​∑k=1K|g^k−gk∗|2≤α1rms,\|\hat{\mathbf{g}}-\mathbf{g}^{*}\|_{\mathbf{p}}\;=\;\sqrt{\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\bigl|\hat{g}_{k}-g_{k}^{*}\bigr|^{2}}\;\leq\;\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}}, (124)

where α1rms\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}} is the RMS upper bound from (98), given by

α1rms=3​Δρ​ρ^maxK⏟proxy term+2​E+​ρ^max​ℓmax​∑iρ^i​ℓiK​ℓ¯⏟off-diagonal Gram term+E+​ℓmax​∑iρ^i​ℓiK​ℓ¯ 2⏟aggregate off-diagonal term.\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}}\;=\;\underbrace{\frac{3\,\Delta_{\rho}\,\hat{\rho}_{\max}}{\sqrt{K}}}_{\text{proxy term}}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{2\,E_{+}\,\sqrt{\hat{\rho}_{\max}\,\ell_{\max}\,\sum_{i}\hat{\rho}_{i}\,\ell_{i}}}{\sqrt{K}\,\bar{\ell}}}_{\text{off-diagonal Gram term}}\;+\;\underbrace{\frac{E_{+}\,\ell_{\max}\,\sum_{i}\hat{\rho}_{i}\,\ell_{i}}{K\,\bar{\ell}^{\,2}}}_{\text{aggregate off-diagonal term}}. (125)

The constant α1\alpha_{1} in Lemma 12 is recovered as α1=(α1rms)2/4\alpha_{1}=(\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}})^{2}/4.

Proof.

By the triangle inequality, ‖𝐠^−𝐠∗‖𝐩≤‖𝜼prox‖𝐩+‖𝜼diag‖𝐩\|\hat{\mathbf{g}}-\mathbf{g}^{*}\|_{\mathbf{p}}\leq\|\boldsymbol{\eta}_{\mathrm{prox}}\|_{\mathbf{p}}+\|\boldsymbol{\eta}_{\mathrm{diag}}\|_{\mathbf{p}}, where 𝜼prox\boldsymbol{\eta}_{\mathrm{prox}} and 𝜼diag\boldsymbol{\eta}_{\mathrm{diag}} are defined in the proof of Lemma 12. Combining the bounds in (89) and (96) gives (124), with α1rms\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}} given by (125). ∎

The three terms in (125) correspond to the three sources of surrogate error. The first term, 3​Δρ​ρ^max/K3\Delta_{\rho}\hat{\rho}_{\max}/\sqrt{K}, is the proxy-substitution error: it comes from replacing the exact per-trajectory rates ρi∗\rho_{i}^{*} in the closed form of gk∗g_{k}^{*} by the forward-pass proxies ρ^i\hat{\rho}_{i}. Its size is controlled by Δρ\Delta_{\rho}, which measures the multiplicative gap between ρi∗\rho_{i}^{*} and ρ^i\hat{\rho}_{i} in Lemma 11. The second term, 2​E+​ρ^max​ℓmax​∑iρ^i​ℓi/(K​ℓ¯)2E_{+}\sqrt{\hat{\rho}_{\max}\ell_{\max}\sum_{i}\hat{\rho}_{i}\ell_{i}}/(\sqrt{K}\,\bar{\ell}), controls the per-coordinate off-diagonal Gram residual ok=𝐠k⊤​𝐠¯−‖𝐠k‖2/Ko_{k}=\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{g}}-\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}/K, which is ignored by the diagonal approximation 𝐠k⊤​𝐠¯≈‖𝐠k‖2/K\mathbf{g}_{k}^{\top}\bar{\mathbf{g}}\approx\|\mathbf{g}_{k}\|^{2}/K. The third term, E+​ℓmax​∑iρ^i​ℓi/(K​ℓ¯2)E_{+}\ell_{\max}\sum_{i}\hat{\rho}_{i}\ell_{i}/(K\bar{\ell}^{2}), controls the aggregate off-diagonal mass O=‖𝐠¯‖2−K−2​∑i‖𝐠i‖2O=\|\bar{\mathbf{g}}\|^{2}-K^{-2}\sum_{i}\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2} left over by the approximation ‖𝐠¯‖2≈K−2​∑i‖𝐠i‖2\|\bar{\mathbf{g}}\|^{2}\approx K^{-2}\sum_{i}\|\mathbf{g}_{i}\|^{2}. The latter two terms are small when the per-trajectory gradients are close to orthogonal in parameter space.

The bound in (124) is an aggregate RMS bound across the KK candidates, not a per-coordinate guarantee. By the equivalence of finite-dimensional norms,

maxk∈[K]⁡|g^k−gk∗|≤∑k=1K|g^k−gk∗|2=K​‖𝐠^−𝐠∗‖𝐩≤K​α1rms.\max_{k\in[K]}|\hat{g}_{k}-g_{k}^{*}|\;\leq\;\sqrt{\sum_{k=1}^{K}|\hat{g}_{k}-g_{k}^{*}|^{2}}\;=\;\sqrt{K}\,\|\hat{\mathbf{g}}-\mathbf{g}^{*}\|_{\mathbf{p}}\;\leq\;\sqrt{K}\,\alpha_{1}^{\mathrm{rms}}. (126)

Thus a single coordinate can have a larger error in the worst case, while the RMS error remains controlled. This RMS norm is the relevant quantity for the residual analysis because the Cauchy–Schwarz step in (83) naturally pairs χ2(𝐪∥𝐩)\sqrt{\chi^{2}(\mathbf{q}\|\mathbf{p})} with ‖𝜼‖𝐩\|\boldsymbol{\eta}\|_{\mathbf{p}}.

B.8.2 Empirical Correlation between 𝐠^\hat{\mathbf{g}} and 𝐠∗\mathbf{g}^{*}

The bound in Corollary 3 is a worst-case guarantee whose constants depend on the structural quantities of Lemma 11. We complement this analysis by directly measuring how well 𝐠^\hat{\mathbf{g}} tracks 𝐠∗\mathbf{g}^{*} on a real student model.

We sample 5050 questions uniformly from the candidate pool described in Appendix C.1. For each question, we compute both the LARK surrogate g^k\hat{g}_{k} and the exact directional derivative gk∗=∂ρ⁡(𝜽ref,𝐪)/∂qk|𝐪=𝐩g_{k}^{*}=\partial\rho(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}};\mathbf{q})/\partial q_{k}|_{\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{p}}. The exact derivative is obtained by one full-parameter backward pass per candidate trajectory at the anchor model 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}} (Qwen-2.5-7B), rather than by a low-rank or kernel approximation. Across 5050 questions and K=33K=33 candidates per question, this produces 1,6501{,}650 paired values (g^k,gk∗)(\hat{g}_{k},g_{k}^{*}). To compare values across questions, we apply a per-question affine rescaling that aligns the mean and scale of g^k\hat{g}_{k} with those of gk∗g_{k}^{*}. This rescaling preserves within-question rankings and therefore does not affect Recall​@​B\mathrm{Recall@}B.

We report three metrics. First, we compute pooled Pearson rr and Spearman ρ\rho between the rescaled g^k\hat{g}_{k} and gk∗g_{k}^{*} to measure scalar agreement. Second, because LARK uses 𝐠^\hat{\mathbf{g}} primarily through its top-BB ranking, we report Recall​@​B≜|topB​(𝐠^)∩topB​(𝐠∗)|/B\mathrm{Recall@}B\triangleq|\mathrm{top}_{B}(\hat{\mathbf{g}})\cap\mathrm{top}_{B}(\mathbf{g}^{*})|/B averaged over questions for B∈{1,…,10}B\in\{1,\ldots,10\}, with random baseline B/KB/K. Third, we report the per-question relative 𝐩\mathbf{p}-weighted RMS error ‖𝐠^−𝐠∗‖𝐩/‖𝐠∗‖𝐩\|\hat{\mathbf{g}}-\mathbf{g}^{*}\|_{\mathbf{p}}/\|\mathbf{g}^{*}\|_{\mathbf{p}}, matching the norm used in Corollary 3.

Figure 6(a) shows a clear positive relationship between g^k\hat{g}_{k} and gk∗g_{k}^{*}, with pooled Pearson r=0.748r=0.748 and Spearman ρ=0.566\rho=0.566. This indicates that the surrogate captures a substantial portion of the scalar variation in gk∗g_{k}^{*} after per-question affine rescaling, while the remaining gap is consistent with the off-diagonal Gram interactions omitted by the diagonal approximation in (125).

The ranking agreement is also substantially above chance. As shown in Figure 6(b), Recall​@​1≈0.38\mathrm{Recall@}1\approx 0.38, far above the random baseline 1/K≈0.031/K\approx 0.03. At the main experimental budget B=3B=3, Recall​@​3≈0.56\mathrm{Recall@}3\approx 0.56, compared with the random baseline 3/K≈0.093/K\approx 0.09. The recall remains around 0.60.6 for larger budgets, indicating that 𝐠^\hat{\mathbf{g}} preserves meaningful top-BB ranking information for the selection rule used by LARK. The error bars also show nontrivial question-level variation, so this result should be interpreted as strong aggregate alignment rather than a perfect per-question match.

Figure 6(c) shows that the relative 𝐩\mathbf{p}-weighted RMS error concentrates around 0.60.6 (mean 0.5740.574, median 0.5900.590), which is far below the loose worst-case per-coordinate factor K≈5.7\sqrt{K}\approx 5.7 allowed by (126). The empirical error is therefore much smaller than the theoretical worst case, as expected in non-adversarial candidate pools.

Overall, these diagnostics support the use of 𝐠^\hat{\mathbf{g}} as a forward-pass surrogate for top-BB trajectory selection. The surrogate is not a high-precision coordinate-wise estimator of 𝐠∗\mathbf{g}^{*}, but it is positively aligned with 𝐠∗\mathbf{g}^{*} at the scalar level and preserves useful top-BB ranking information. This is the operative notion of agreement for LARK, since the closed-form selection rule in Lemma 3 depends on the top-BB ordering and the score margins above the threshold, rather than on the exact magnitude of every coordinate. The empirical results therefore support the computational tradeoff made by LARK: avoiding KK full-parameter backward passes per question while retaining the ranking signal needed for downstream selection.

Appendix C Experimental Details

C.1 Candidate Pool

We adopt the trajectory candidate pool released by Yang et al. [2026] without modification. The pool consists of 5,000 mathematical reasoning problems sampled from NuminaMath [Li et al., 2024], each paired with 33 reasoning trajectories produced by 11 teacher models with 3 independent rollouts per teacher. All selection methods in our experiments—including LARK and every baseline in Appendix C.2—operate on this identical pool, so any difference in downstream performance is attributable to the selection rule rather than to differences in the underlying candidate set.

Teacher pool.

The 11 teacher models span a range of scales and model families, including both proprietary and open-weight reasoning models: GPT-OSS-20B, GPT-OSS-120B, Phi-4-R+, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-235B, Qwen3-30B, Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, Nemotron, and Magistral-S. For each (problem, teacher) pair, three independent rollouts are generated, yielding 11×3=3311\times 3=33 trajectories per problem. We refer the reader to Yang et al. [2026] for the full inference configuration of each teacher (decoding temperature, top-pp, maximum generation length).

Correctness filtering.

Every trajectory retained in the pool has been verified to reach the correct final answer under the extraction rule of Yang et al. [2026], which matches the rule described in Appendix C.4. Trajectories whose final answer disagrees with the ground truth are not included. As a result, all 33 candidates for each problem are correct reasoning trajectories that nonetheless differ in reasoning style, length, and student-side learnability—a setting that isolates the selection problem from the orthogonal question of correctness verification.

C.2 Trajectory Selection Baselines

We compare LARK against the seven baselines reported in Table 1. Throughout this subsection, let 𝐱\mathbf{x} denote the prompt (system and user turns), and let {𝐲k}k=1K\{\mathbf{y}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K} with K=33K=33 denote the candidate trajectories for 𝐱\mathbf{x} in the pool 𝒞⁡(𝐱)\mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}) described in Appendix C.1. Each trajectory has length |ak||a_{k}|, with tt-th token ytky_{t}^{k}, predictive distribution 𝝅tk=π𝜽(⋅∣𝐱,𝐲<tk)∈Δ|𝒱|\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}=\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}_{<t}^{k})\in\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|} under the student π𝜽\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}, ground-truth one-hot 𝜹⁡(ytk)∈Δ|𝒱|\boldsymbol{\delta}(y_{t}^{k})\in\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|}, and length-normalized cross-entropy ℓk=1|ak|∑t=1|ak|−log𝝅tk(ytk)\ell_{k}=\tfrac{1}{|a_{k}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|a_{k}|}-\log\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}(y_{t}^{k}). Each baseline assigns a scalar score to every candidate 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k} and selects the top-BB trajectories under that score with uniform weights 1/B1/B; LARK instead applies its closed-form χ2\chi^{2}-BB rule to obtain non-uniform weights.

Random.

We sample one trajectory uniformly at random from {𝐲k}k=1K\{\mathbf{y}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}:

𝐲⋆∼Uniform⁡({𝐲k}k=1K).\mathbf{y}^{\star}\sim\mathrm{Uniform}\bigl(\{\mathbf{y}_{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}\bigr).

For B>1B>1, we sample BB trajectories without replacement.

Token Lengthmax.

We score each candidate by its token length and select the longest:

scorelen​(𝐲k)≜|ak|,𝐲⋆=arg⁡maxk∈[K]​scorelen​(𝐲k).\mathrm{score}_{\text{len}}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\triangleq|a_{k}|,\qquad\mathbf{y}^{\star}=\arg\max_{k\in[K]}\mathrm{score}_{\text{len}}(\mathbf{y}_{k}).
Rule-based Qualitymax (LIMO-style).

We implement a lightweight heuristic inspired by LIMO-style filtering [Ye et al., 2025], combining four indicators computed from the assistant text of 𝐲k\mathbf{y}_{k}: (i) elaborated reasoning (total word length), (ii) self-verification (frequency of “check” and “verify”), (iii) exploratory approach (frequency of “perhaps” and “might”), (iv) adaptive granularity (frequency of “therefore” and “since”). For each candidate, the frequency of each keyword group is normalized by the total word count. We zz-score each indicator across the KK candidates within the same pool and take a weighted sum:

scorerule​(𝐲k)=0.30⋅z⁡(len)+0.20⋅z⁡(selfver)+0.25⋅z⁡(explore)+0.25⋅z⁡(granularity),\mathrm{score}_{\text{rule}}(\mathbf{y}_{k})=0.30\cdot z(\mathrm{len})+0.20\cdot z(\mathrm{selfver})+0.25\cdot z(\mathrm{explore})+0.25\cdot z(\mathrm{granularity}),

where z⁡(⋅)z(\cdot) denotes within-pool zz-scoring. We select 𝐲⋆=arg⁡maxk∈[K]​scorerule​(𝐲k)\mathbf{y}^{\star}=\arg\max_{k\in[K]}\mathrm{score}_{\text{rule}}(\mathbf{y}_{k}).

LLM-judged Qualitymax.

We use Qwen3-32B-Instruct [Yang et al., 2025] as a judge model in non-thinking mode. Given (𝐱,𝐲k)(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}_{k}), the judge outputs a JSON object with an overall_score sjudge​(𝐲k)∈[0,1]s_{\text{judge}}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\in[0,1] and a textual overall_reason. We select 𝐲⋆=arg⁡maxk∈[K]​sjudge​(𝐲k)\mathbf{y}^{\star}=\arg\max_{k\in[K]}s_{\text{judge}}(\mathbf{y}_{k}). The verbatim judge prompt is given below.

Global Naturalness (GRAPE)max [Zhang et al., 2025a].

GRAPE scores each candidate by the average log-likelihood assigned to its tokens by the student under teacher forcing, equivalently the negative length-normalized cross-entropy:

scoreGRAPE​(𝐲k)≜−ℓk=1|ak|​∑t=1|ak|log⁡𝝅tk​(ytk).\mathrm{score}_{\text{GRAPE}}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\;\triangleq\;-\,\ell_{k}\;=\;\frac{1}{|a_{k}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|a_{k}|}\log\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}(y_{t}^{k}).

We select 𝐲⋆=arg⁡maxk∈[K]​scoreGRAPE​(𝐲k)\mathbf{y}^{\star}=\arg\max_{k\in[K]}\mathrm{score}_{\text{GRAPE}}(\mathbf{y}_{k}), which is equivalent to selecting the trajectory of minimum length-normalized cross-entropy under the student.

Local Naturalnessmax [Just et al., 2025].

We follow the Local Naturalness metric. Each trajectory is split into JkJ_{k} sentence-level steps 𝐲k=(𝐬1,…,𝐬Jk)\mathbf{y}_{k}=(\mathbf{s}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{s}_{J_{k}}), where each 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j} is a contiguous sub-sequence of tokens. With local context size mm (we use m=4m=4), we compute

scorelocal(𝐲k)≜1Jk∑j=1Jk(1|𝐬j|∑u=1|𝐬j|logπ𝜽(sj,u|𝐱,𝐬j−m:j−1,𝐬j,<u)),\mathrm{score}_{\text{local}}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\;\triangleq\;\frac{1}{J_{k}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{k}}\!\left(\frac{1}{|\mathbf{s}_{j}|}\sum_{u=1}^{|\mathbf{s}_{j}|}\log\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\!\left(s_{j,u}\,\big|\,\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{s}_{j-m:j-1},\,\mathbf{s}_{j,<u}\right)\right),

where 𝐬j−m:j−1\mathbf{s}_{j-m:j-1} denotes up to mm immediately preceding steps and sj,us_{j,u} is the uu-th token of step 𝐬j\mathbf{s}_{j}. We select 𝐲⋆=arg⁡maxk∈[K]​scorelocal​(𝐲k)\mathbf{y}^{\star}=\arg\max_{k\in[K]}\mathrm{score}_{\text{local}}(\mathbf{y}_{k}). Unlike GRAPE, this score requires m+1m+1 forward passes per trajectory (one per masked-context rollout); see Appendix D.1.

Rank-Surprisal Ratio (RSR)min [Yang et al., 2026].

RSR computes token-level surprisal and rank under the student. For each token ytky_{t}^{k} with context 𝐜tk=(𝐱,𝐲<tk)\mathbf{c}_{t}^{k}=(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}_{<t}^{k}), define the surprisal and rank as

stk≜−log𝝅tk(ytk),rtk≜ 1+∑v∈𝒱𝕀[π𝜽(v∣𝐜tk)>𝝅tk(ytk)].s_{t}^{k}\;\triangleq\;-\log\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}(y_{t}^{k}),\qquad r_{t}^{k}\;\triangleq\;1+\!\!\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}\!\!\mathbb{I}\!\left[\pi_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(v\mid\mathbf{c}_{t}^{k})>\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}(y_{t}^{k})\right].

Ranks are clipped at rmaxr_{\max} (we use rmax=100r_{\max}=100): r¯tk≜min⁡(rtk,rmax)\bar{r}_{t}^{k}\triangleq\min(r_{t}^{k},r_{\max}). The trajectory-level score is

scoreRSR​(𝐲k)≜∑t=1|ak|r¯tk∑t=1|ak|stk,𝐲⋆=arg⁡mink∈[K]​scoreRSR​(𝐲k).\mathrm{score}_{\text{RSR}}(\mathbf{y}_{k})\;\triangleq\;\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{|a_{k}|}\bar{r}_{t}^{k}}{\sum_{t=1}^{|a_{k}|}s_{t}^{k}},\qquad\mathbf{y}^{\star}=\arg\min_{k\in[K]}\mathrm{score}_{\text{RSR}}(\mathbf{y}_{k}).

Surprisal and clipped rank are computed from a single forward pass; clipping at rmaxr_{\max} avoids the O⁡(|𝒱|)O(|\mathcal{V}|) full sort while remaining exact (Appendix C.3).

C.3 Implementation Details

SFT training.

We use a single hyperparameter recipe across all three students (Qwen-2.5-7B, Qwen-2.5-1.5B, Llama-3.2-3B) and across all selection methods, so that any difference in downstream performance can be attributed to the selection rule rather than to per-method training tuning. Each student is fine-tuned with full-parameter SFT under the following configuration:

  • •

    Maximum sequence length: 32,76832{,}768 tokens, kept identical across selection scoring, SFT, and evaluation; trajectories exceeding this length (less than 1%1\% of the pool) are truncated from the right.

  • •

    Learning rate: 1.0×10−51.0\times 10^{-5} for the main 5,0005{,}000-trajectory experiments and 5.0×10−65.0\times 10^{-6} for the 500500-trajectory verification of Condition 1 in Appendix A.3, linearly scaled to the smaller dataset to avoid early-step instability.

  • •

    Effective global batch size: 6464 trajectories, realized as 88 GPUs ×\times per-device batch 11 ×\times gradient accumulation 88.

  • •

    Epochs: 55.

  • •

    Optimizer: AdamW (PyTorch implementation) with default (β1,β2,ε)=(0.9,0.999,10−8)(\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\varepsilon)=(0.9,0.999,10^{-8}) and weight decay 00.

  • •

    Learning-rate schedule: cosine decay with linear warm-up over the first 5%5\% of total steps.

  • •

    Gradient clipping: max-norm 1.01.0, delegated to DeepSpeed via gradient_clipping: auto.

  • •

    Precision: bf16 mixed precision throughout, with fp32 communication for ZeRO collectives. We disable bf16 reduced-precision matmul accumulation (torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_bf16_reduced_precision_reduction == False) to suppress occasional NaN gradients in the LM-head backward on A100; fp16 is never used.

  • •

    Memory and throughput optimizations: non-reentrant gradient checkpointing, FlashAttention-2, sequence packing with greedy bin-packing and reset position_ids, and Liger fused kernels (RoPE, RMSNorm, SwiGLU). The fused linear-CE kernel is disabled because it is incompatible with sequence packing.

Software stack.

Training and inference run inside a single conda environment with PyTorch 2.9.12.9.1 (CUDA 12.812.8), Transformers 4.57.14.57.1, PEFT 0.18.00.18.0, FlashAttention 2.8.32.8.3, Liger-Kernel, and DeepSpeed. Distributed training is launched via torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 on top of the HuggingFace Trainer, using DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 22 (zero2_bf16.json: stage 2, communication_data_type fp32, reduce/allgather_bucket_size =5×108=5\times 10^{8}). Under ZeRO-22, optimizer states and gradients are sharded across the 88 GPUs while parameters are replicated, which is sufficient for the ≤8\leq 8B-parameter students considered. Evaluation uses vLLM 0.15.00.15.0 for batched multi-sample decoding, with SGLang 0.5.90.5.9 available as a fallback engine.

Hardware and wall-clock.

All experiments run on a single node with 8×8\times NVIDIA A100 80GB (SXM4) GPUs. Each 5,0005{,}000-trajectory SFT run completes in roughly 33–55 hours depending on the student size, and each 500500-trajectory verification run for Appendix D.2 completes in about 2525–4545 minutes. Aggregating across 33 students, 77 selection baselines (Appendix C.2), and the LARK ablation grid (top-B∈{1,3,5,10}B\in\{1,3,5,10\} together with χ2\chi^{2}- and KL-tempered weighting variants), the total training budget is approximately 1,6001{,}600 A100-hours. Evaluation is sharded across the same 88 GPUs with tensor_parallel_size=1=1 per shard, with generations merged across shards afterwards, adding on average ∼15\sim 15 minutes per (student, benchmark) pair.

Prompt consistency and truncation.

A single chat template is applied throughout the pipeline. The same tokenizer.apply_chat_template call is used for (i) selection-time scoring (when computing the forward-pass quantities ρ^k\hat{\rho}_{k} and g^k\hat{g}_{k} on candidate trajectories under 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}}), (ii) SFT example construction (masking out the system and user turns so that only the assistant turn contributes to the loss), and (iii) evaluation prompting (generation prompt appended via add_generation_prompt=True). All three stages truncate to the same 32,76832{,}768-token limit. The reasoning instruction "Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}" is held fixed across selection, training, and evaluation, ensuring that selection scores measured on 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}} remain meaningful for the fine-tuned model under matched prompting.

Reproducibility.

We fix the global seed to 4242 for random, numpy, and torch in all selection-scoring and Condition 1 verification experiments, and rely on the HuggingFace Trainer default seed of 4242 for SFT. All headline numbers in Table 1 are reported as the mean ±\pm standard deviation over 33 independent evaluation runs that differ only in the sampling seed of the inference engine, with decoding hyperparameters temperature=0.6=0.6, top_p=0.95=0.95, repetition_penalty=1.1=1.1, and maximum generation length 32,76832{,}768, evaluated under ACC@55 with 55 samples per problem (Appendix C.4). To facilitate reproduction we will release, under an MIT licence, the full training code, the YAML configuration files (train/configs/sft_full.yaml, train/configs/sft_full_500.yaml, train/configs/zero2_bf16.json), the precomputed per-trajectory scores (data/Q1/<student>/grape_g/scores.json), and the selection rules used in each ablation.

C.4 Evaluation Protocol

Benchmarks.

We evaluate on the same four reasoning benchmarks reported in Section 5.1, which span competition mathematics, grade-level mathematics, and graduate-level science: AIME-2024 [, 2024] (3030 problems from the 20242024 American Invitational Mathematics Examination), AMC [Mathematical Association of America, 2025] (8383 problems from the American Mathematics Competitions), MATH-500 [Hendrycks et al., 2021] (500500 problems sampled from the MATH test set, which covers algebra, geometry, number theory, probability, and precalculus), and GPQA-Diamond [Rein et al., 2024] (198198 multiple-choice questions written by domain experts in physics, chemistry, and biology). The four benchmarks together cover both numeric-answer and multiple-choice formats, which lets us assess whether the improvements brought by LARK transfer beyond the mathematical reasoning domain on which the candidate pool is constructed. The Avg column in Table 1 is the unweighted mean of these four benchmarks; because the four splits differ in the number of problems, the per-benchmark numbers remain the primary basis of comparison.

Decoding configuration.

For every benchmark and every fine-tuned student, we generate 55 independent samples per problem with the following decoding parameters:

  • •

    temperature =0.6=0.6

  • •

    top-p=0.95p=0.95

  • •

    top-k=−1k=-1 (no top-kk truncation)

  • •

    maximum generation length == 32,76832{,}768 tokens (matching the SFT context length)

The same decoding configuration is used across all baselines and LARK to ensure that any difference in downstream accuracy is attributable to the selection rule rather than to inference-time differences.

Metric (ACC@5).

We report ACC@5 as our primary evaluation metric. For each test problem, we sample 55 independent generations under the decoding configuration above; the problem is marked correct if any of the 55 generations contains the correct final answer under the extraction rule described below. ACC@5 captures whether the student model is capable of producing a correct reasoning trajectory for the problem within a small sampling budget, and is less sensitive to single-sample variance than greedy ACC@1. Each experiment is repeated under three independent decoding seeds, with the selected training data and the SFT seed held fixed; we report the mean and standard deviation of ACC@5 across these three decoding seeds, so the reported variability captures inference-time sampling noise rather than training-seed noise.

System prompts.

We use a fixed system prompt per benchmark family, distinguishing numeric-answer tasks (AIME, AMC), multiple-choice tasks (GPQA), and free-form-answer tasks (MATH-500). All three prompts share the same overall structure — enforcing English output, separating the reasoning chain from the final answer, and requiring the answer in a \boxed{...} environment for unambiguous extraction — and differ only in the answer-format specification.

Answer extraction rule.

We extract the predicted final answer from each generation using the following deterministic rule:

  • •

    If the generation contains at least one \boxed{...} token, we take the content inside the last \boxed{...} as the predicted answer. The last (rather than first) occurrence is used because models occasionally produce intermediate boxed expressions during reasoning; only the final boxed value is treated as the answer.

  • •

    If the generation contains no \boxed{...} token, the generation is treated as incorrect, regardless of whether the surrounding text contains a correct value.

For numeric-answer tasks (AIME, AMC), the extracted string is canonicalized by stripping surrounding whitespace and converting fractions a/ba/b to their decimal form before comparison with the ground truth. For multiple-choice tasks (GPQA), the extracted string is uppercased and compared against the gold letter in {A,B,C,D}\{\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B},\mathrm{C},\mathrm{D}\}. For free-form answers (MATH-500), we follow the canonicalization rules of Hendrycks et al. [2021], which normalize fraction, square-root, and exponent notation prior to string matching.

Efficient scoring for rank-based metrics.

The RSR baseline of Appendix C.2 requires the clipped rank r¯tk=min⁡(rtk,rmax)\bar{r}_{t}^{k}=\min(r_{t}^{k},r_{\max}) at every token position. A naive implementation would sort the full |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|-dimensional logit vector at each token, costing O⁡(|𝒱|​log⁡|𝒱|)O(|\mathcal{V}|\log|\mathcal{V}|) per token. We avoid this by observing that under rank clipping at rmaxr_{\max}, only the relative order of the top-rmaxr_{\max} logits matters: any token whose true rank exceeds rmaxr_{\max} is mapped to rmaxr_{\max} regardless of its exact rank. We therefore extract the top-rmaxr_{\max} logits via torch.topk (cost O⁡(|𝒱|​log⁡rmax)O(|\mathcal{V}|\log r_{\max}) per token), check whether the gold token ytky_{t}^{k} is among them, and assign r¯tk\bar{r}_{t}^{k} accordingly. This procedure is exact under rank clipping and reduces the per-token cost by a factor of log⁡|𝒱|/log⁡rmax\log|\mathcal{V}|/\log r_{\max}, which is roughly 5×5\times–6×6\times for |𝒱|≈1.5×105|\mathcal{V}|\approx 1.5\times 10^{5} and rmax=100r_{\max}=100. The same forward pass that produces the surprisal stk=−log⁡𝝅tk​(ytk)s_{t}^{k}=-\log\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}(y_{t}^{k}) is reused to produce the top-rmaxr_{\max} logits, so RSR scoring requires only one forward pass per candidate trajectory.

Prompt consistency.

We use a consistent chat template across (i) selection-time scoring (when the student model evaluates each candidate trajectory under teacher forcing), (ii) SFT loss formatting (when the model is fine-tuned on the selected trajectories), and (iii) evaluation-time prompting (when the fine-tuned model is queried on benchmark problems). Using the same chat template at all three stages reduces train–test mismatch and ensures that selection scores measured on 𝜽ref\boldsymbol{\theta}_{\mathrm{ref}} remain meaningful for the fine-tuned model. All inputs are truncated to the same maximum sequence length of 32,76832{,}768 tokens used for SFT.

C.5 Train/Eval Contamination Audit

To ensure that the downstream evaluation results in Table 1 reflect genuine generalization rather than memorization of training-time supervision, we audit the overlap between the 5,0005{,}000-problem NuminaMath candidate pool of Appendix C.1 and every problem in the evaluation benchmarks of Appendix C.4.

Method.

For each evaluation problem we compute the character 88-gram Jaccard similarity against every problem in the candidate pool, after a normalization step that lowercases the text, collapses whitespace, and strips redundant LaTeX spacing macros. We report two statistics: (i) exact matches (Jaccard =1=1 after normalization), which would indicate verbatim duplication; and (ii) near-matches at three progressively stricter thresholds, J≥0.4J\geq 0.4, J≥0.7J\geq 0.7, and J≥0.85J\geq 0.85, to capture different degrees of surface overlap. The metric is sensitive to both surface and structural duplication: an exact-template variant with all numerals changed typically scores J∈[0.7,0.95]J\in[0.7,0.95], while a fully independent problem on the same topic typically scores J<0.2J<0.2.

Results.

Table 2 summarizes the audit across all four evaluation benchmarks (AIME-2024, AMC, GPQA-Diamond, and MATH-500, broken down by difficulty levels L1–L5). The audit detects 𝟎\mathbf{0} exact matches across all 811811 evaluation problems. AIME-2024, AMC, GPQA-Diamond, and MATH-L1 contain 00 near-matches at every threshold; GPQA-Diamond is graduate-level physics, chemistry, and biology with no domain overlap with the math-only NuminaMath training pool, while AIME, AMC, and MATH-L1 simply do not appear in the pool under any threshold. MATH-L2 through L5 contain 3131 near-matches at J≥0.4J\geq 0.4 (∼3.7%\sim 3.7\% of the MATH-500 split), of which only 11 case at J≥0.85J\geq 0.85.

Categorization of MATH-L2–L5 near-matches.

Manual inspection of all 3131 flagged pairs places them in three categories, none of which constitute contamination:

  1. 1.

    Template-shared, numerically perturbed. Same algebraic template, different constants or signs, leading to a different polynomial and a different answer. The highest-similarity case (MATH-L2 #11, J=0.869J=0.869) asks for the smallest nn such that all roots of z4+z2+1=0z^{4}+z^{2}+1=0 are nn-th roots of unity, while the closest training problem asks the same question for z4−z2+1=0z^{4}-z^{2}+1=0.

  2. 2.

    Template-shared, different question on the same setup. Same physical or geometric setup, but a different quantity is asked, with no derivable relation between the two answers. For example, MATH-L5 #46 (J=0.693J=0.693) describes a hot-air balloon held by four ropes anchored at points A,B,C,DA,B,C,D; the training problem on the same setup asks for the length of O​HOH, whereas the evaluation problem asks for the greatest rope length saved by replacing H​C+H​DHC+HD with a single rope at a chosen point. These are companion problems from the parent MATH dataset.

  3. 3.

    Surface-level template variation. Same problem stem with different numerical inputs (e.g., coefficients in a quadratic completion task). MATH-L4 #38 (J=0.664J=0.664) asks to rewrite x2+2.6​x+3.6x^{2}+2.6x+3.6 in the form (x+b)2+c(x+b)^{2}+c, while the training problem performs the same operation on x2−20​x+36x^{2}-20x+36. The procedure is identical but the inputs and outputs differ.

In none of the 3131 flagged cases does the answer to a training problem transfer to the corresponding evaluation problem, and no exact duplicates of any AIME-2024, AMC, GPQA-Diamond, or MATH-500 problem appear in the training pool. The downstream Acc@5 results in Table 1 therefore reflect generalization to held-out problems rather than retrieval of memorized supervision.

Appendix D Diagnostic Analyses of LARK

This appendix collects additional evaluation results and diagnostic analyses that validate the design choices of LARK beyond the main downstream comparison. Appendix D.1 verifies the efficiency claim through both an asymptotic complexity derivation and a wall-clock measurement on 88 A100 GPUs, showing that LARK matches the lowest cost achieved by any per-trajectory scoring baseline. Appendix D.2 sweeps the selection budget BB from 1 to 20 on a 500-problem diagnostic subset and studies how performance changes with the budget. Appendix D.3 zooms into a single training problem to illustrate, end to end, the score landscape over candidate trajectories, the token-level structure of the chosen trajectory, the χ2\chi^{2}-BB weighting it induces, and the resulting weighted SFT objective for that problem.

D.1 Computational Cost

We separate every per-trajectory score into two parts: a single forward pass over the trajectory through the student model, with cost Cfwd​(|ak|)C_{\mathrm{fwd}}(|a_{k}|), and a per-token post-processing step on the resulting logits. Decomposing the total cost in this way exposes the differences across methods, which would otherwise be hidden by the dominant forward-pass term.

Per-trajectory cost decomposition.

A single forward pass through a transformer with LL layers, hidden dimension dd, and vocabulary size |𝒱||\mathcal{V}| on a trajectory of length |ak||a_{k}| has cost

Cfwd​(|ak|)=𝒪⁡(L​|ak|​d2)⏟MLP+𝒪⁡(L​|ak|2​d)⏟attention+𝒪⁡(|ak|⋅|𝒱|⋅d)⏟LM head.\displaystyle C_{\mathrm{fwd}}(|a_{k}|)=\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(L|a_{k}|d^{2})}_{\text{MLP}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(L|a_{k}|^{2}d)}_{\text{attention}}+\underbrace{\mathcal{O}(|a_{k}|\cdot|\mathcal{V}|\cdot d)}_{\text{LM head}}.

After this forward pass, every per-trajectory selection method applies a post-processing operation to the logits at each token. GRAPE computes the cross-entropy of the gold token from a |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|-dimensional log-sum-exp, with per-token cost 𝒪⁡(|𝒱|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|). LARK computes both the cross-entropy and the Brier component ∑v𝝅tk​(v)2\sum_{v}\boldsymbol{\pi}_{t}^{k}(v)^{2}, again with per-token cost 𝒪⁡(|𝒱|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|). RSR additionally selects the top-rmaxr_{\max} entries of each token distribution to form a partial rank statistic, with per-token cost 𝒪⁡(|𝒱|​log⁡rmax)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|\log r_{\max}). Local Naturalness instead runs m+1m+1 independent forward passes per trajectory (one for each masked rollout), each followed by an 𝒪⁡(|𝒱|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|) per-token operation.

Total complexity.

Let NN denote the number of training problems and KK the number of candidate trajectories per problem. Aggregating the forward and the post-processing terms over all N​KNK candidates yields the total cost of each method:

GRAPE:\displaystyle\text{GRAPE}\!:\quad 𝒪⁡(N​K⋅[Cfwd​(|ak|)+|ak|⋅|𝒱|]),\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\!\big(NK\cdot[C_{\mathrm{fwd}}(|a_{k}|)+|a_{k}|\cdot|\mathcal{V}|]\big),
LARK:\displaystyle\text{LARK}\!:\quad 𝒪⁡(N​K⋅[Cfwd​(|ak|)+|ak|⋅|𝒱|]),\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\!\big(NK\cdot[C_{\mathrm{fwd}}(|a_{k}|)+|a_{k}|\cdot|\mathcal{V}|]\big),
RSR:\displaystyle\text{RSR}\!:\quad 𝒪⁡(N​K⋅[Cfwd​(|ak|)+|ak|⋅|𝒱|​log⁡rmax]),\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\!\big(NK\cdot[C_{\mathrm{fwd}}(|a_{k}|)+|a_{k}|\cdot|\mathcal{V}|\log r_{\max}]\big),
Local Naturalness:\displaystyle\text{Local Naturalness}\!:\quad 𝒪⁡(N​K⋅[(m+1)​Cfwd​(|ak|)+|ak|⋅|𝒱|]).\displaystyle\mathcal{O}\!\big(NK\cdot[(m+1)\,C_{\mathrm{fwd}}(|a_{k}|)+|a_{k}|\cdot|\mathcal{V}|]\big).

LARK matches the lowest cost achieved by GRAPE. RSR adds a log⁡rmax\log r_{\max} factor on the per-token term because of its rank selection step, and Local Naturalness multiplies the dominant forward pass by m+1m+1 because of its repeated rollouts. The strict ordering GRAPE=LARK<RSR\text{GRAPE}=\text{LARK}<\text{RSR} and GRAPE=LARK<Local Naturalness\text{GRAPE}=\text{LARK}<\text{Local Naturalness} follows from |ak|⋅|𝒱|<|ak|⋅|𝒱|​log⁡rmax|a_{k}|\cdot|\mathcal{V}|<|a_{k}|\cdot|\mathcal{V}|\log r_{\max} and from Cfwd<(m+1)​CfwdC_{\mathrm{fwd}}<(m+1)\,C_{\mathrm{fwd}} for m≥1m\geq 1. We do not assign a model-independent asymptotic formula to LLM-judged Quality because its cost depends on the judge model and serving setup; we therefore report it in the wall-clock comparison.

Empirical wall-clock cost.

We benchmark each scoring method by measuring its per-sample wall-clock cost on 88 A100 GPUs.22 2 Random, Token Length, and Rule-based Quality require no forward pass through the student and run in negligible time, so we omit them from the figure. Figure 7 reports the resulting cost across all five scoring methods. LARK (1.321.32 s/sample) matches GRAPE (1.281.28 s/sample) to within 3%3\%, which reflects the fact that they share the same forward pass and differ only by an additional 𝒪⁡(|𝒱|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{V}|) Brier sum per token. LLM-judged Quality is 1.6×1.6\times slower at 2.112.11 s/sample because of the auxiliary judge call. RSR is 2.7×2.7\times slower at 3.443.44 s/sample, which is consistent with the extra log⁡rmax\log r_{\max} rank-selection factor in its per-token operation. Local Naturalness is the most expensive at 5.065.06 s/sample, which is 4.0×4.0\times slower than LARK and matches the (m+1)(m+1)-fold forward-pass cost predicted by the asymptotic analysis. The empirical ordering matches the constant-factor ranking implied by the complexity formulas.

D.2 Selection Budget Scaling

We study how LARK behaves as the number of selected trajectories per question changes. This analysis sweeps the selection budget B∈{1,3,5,10,20}B\in\{1,3,5,10,20\} on Qwen-2.5-7B and evaluates the resulting student on AMC Acc@5. Because this sweep is conducted on the same 500-problem subset used for our diagnostic experiments, rather than the full 5,000-problem training set used in Table 1, these results are intended to show the relative trend across budgets rather than to replace the main evaluation results.

For each budget BB, we apply the LARK selection rule to choose BB trajectories per problem, fine-tune Qwen-2.5-7B with the same SFT protocol described in Appendix C, and report AMC Acc@5 in Figure 8. LARK remains effective across the entire budget range: accuracy increases from 49.4%49.4\% at B=1B{=}1 to 65.1%65.1\% at B=3B{=}3, reaches its highest value of 68.7%68.7\% at B=10B{=}10, and remains strong at 66.3%66.3\% when B=20B{=}20.

The trend is not strictly monotonic. Moving from B=1B{=}1 to B=3B{=}3 brings a large improvement, indicating that using multiple selected trajectories can provide complementary supervision. However, increasing the budget beyond B=3B{=}3 gives smaller and less stable gains. In particular, B=5B{=}5 underperforms B=3B{=}3, while B=10B{=}10 gives the best result and B=20B{=}20 slightly decreases. This pattern suggests that a small number of carefully selected trajectories already captures most of the useful training signal, while adding more lower-ranked trajectories can introduce weaker or less informative supervision.

Overall, the budget sweep shows that LARK is not sensitive to a single fixed choice of BB. The method performs well with a small budget (B=3B{=}3) and remains competitive as the budget increases. This supports the use of a small top-BB selection strategy in the main experiments, where the goal is to improve distillation efficiency while avoiding unnecessary supervision from less informative trajectories.

D.3 Case Study: A Single-Problem Walkthrough

While Appendices D.1 and D.2 support the efficiency and budget-scaling analyses of LARK at the aggregate level, this appendix zooms into a single training problem to illustrate the end-to-end behavior of the selection rule. We walk through (i) the problem and its candidate pool, (ii) the LARK score landscape, (iii) the top-1 trajectory selected by LARK, and (iv) the closed-form χ2\chi^{2}-BB weights at B=3B=3.

Problem and candidate pool.

We illustrate on problem pid=839\text{pid}=839 from the candidate pool of Appendix C.1:

The ground-truth answer is 52\boxed{\dfrac{5}{2}}. The pool contains K=33K=33 candidate trajectories produced by 11 teacher models with 3 rollouts each; all reach the correct final answer per the construction of Appendix C.1.

Score landscape.

Figure 9 shows the LARK score g^k\hat{g}_{k} for all 33 candidates, grouped by teacher. The top-1 trajectory is the second rollout of phi4-reason-plus (highlighted in red, g^=0.01782\hat{g}=0.01782); the same teacher’s third rollout takes rank 2 (g^=0.01687\hat{g}=0.01687). Notably, phi4-reason-plus rollout 1 ranks only 25 (g^=0.00960\hat{g}=0.00960): the within-teacher spread on this teacher alone is 1.86×1.86\times, exceeding the spread between several pairs of teachers. The same pattern recurs across the pool (e.g., nemotron-super-v15 rollouts span 0.00520.0052 to 0.00780.0078), which underscores that LARK selects at the trajectory level rather than at the teacher level. Teachers commonly perceived as strong on aggregate benchmarks (deepseek-r1-0528, qwen3-235b-2507, qwq-32b) do not contribute any top-3 trajectory on this problem, with their rollouts clustering near the median.

Top-1 trajectory selected by LARK.

We quote the top-1 trajectory (phi4-reason-plus rollout 2, g^=0.01782\hat{g}=0.01782) in full:

The trajectory is substantially more compact than the average candidate in this pool. Importantly, its length-normalized cross-entropy ℓk\ell_{k} under θref\theta_{\text{ref}} is not the smallest in the pool; what raises g^k\hat{g}_{k} appears to be the structure of the residual rather than low loss alone. A qualitative inspection suggests that high-residual tokens around numeric expressions and key algebraic steps carry a large portion of the cumulative Brier mass, matching the heuristic reading of g^k\hat{g}_{k} in Remark 2.

χ2\chi^{2}-BB weighting at B=3B=3.

With B=3B=3, the closed-form χ2\chi^{2}-BB rule gives the weights from the score margins above the threshold g^(B+1)\hat{g}_{(B+1)}. The four relevant scores on this problem are:

g^(1)\displaystyle\hat{g}_{(1)} =0.01782(phi4-reason-plus.2),\displaystyle=0.01782\quad(\texttt{phi4-reason-plus}.2),
g^(2)\displaystyle\hat{g}_{(2)} =0.01687(phi4-reason-plus.3),\displaystyle=0.01687\quad(\texttt{phi4-reason-plus}.3),
g^(3)\displaystyle\hat{g}_{(3)} =0.01426(gptoss-20b-high.1),\displaystyle=0.01426\quad(\texttt{gptoss-20b-high}.1),
g^(4)\displaystyle\hat{g}_{(4)} =0.01285(gptoss-120b-high.2;threshold).\displaystyle=0.01285\quad(\texttt{gptoss-120b-high}.2;\ \text{threshold}).

The score margins above the threshold are

g^(1)−g^(4)=0.00497,g^(2)−g^(4)=0.00402,g^(3)−g^(4)=0.00141,\hat{g}_{(1)}-\hat{g}_{(4)}=0.00497,\qquad\hat{g}_{(2)}-\hat{g}_{(4)}=0.00402,\qquad\hat{g}_{(3)}-\hat{g}_{(4)}=0.00141,

summing to ∑j=13(g^(j)−g^(4))=0.01040\sum_{j=1}^{3}(\hat{g}_{(j)}-\hat{g}_{(4)})=0.01040. The closed-form temperature is therefore τ∗​(B)=0.01040/K≈3.15×10−4\tau^{*}(B)=0.01040/K\approx 3.15\times 10^{-4}, and the LARK weights are

q^(1)=0.478,q^(2)=0.387,q^(3)=0.136.\hat{q}_{(1)}=0.478,\qquad\hat{q}_{(2)}=0.387,\qquad\hat{q}_{(3)}=0.136.

The contrast with hard top-BB truncation (uniform weight 1/B≈0.3331/B\approx 0.333 each) is substantial: LARK assigns 43%43\% more weight to the rank-1 trajectory than uniform top-3 would, and only 41%41\% as much weight to the rank-3 trajectory. The asymmetry directly reflects the score gap between the two phi4-reason-plus rollouts and the remainder of the pool. The resulting per-problem contribution to the SFT loss is

ℒSFT(pid=839)​(θ)=0.478​ℓ​(θ,𝐲16)+0.387​ℓ​(θ,𝐲17)+0.136​ℓ​(θ,𝐲6),\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}^{(\text{pid}=839)}(\theta)=0.478\,\ell(\theta;\mathbf{y}_{16})+0.387\,\ell(\theta;\mathbf{y}_{17})+0.136\,\ell(\theta;\mathbf{y}_{6}),

with all other 30 candidates carrying zero weight on this problem.

Summary.

The walkthrough illustrates three points anchored at a concrete problem: trajectory-level (rather than teacher-level) variation in g^k\hat{g}_{k} can be the dominant source of selection signal; the LARK-selected trajectory is not the one with the lowest ℓk\ell_{k} but the one with structured residual signal; and the χ2\chi^{2}-BB weighting deviates substantially from uniform top-BB truncation when the top-ranked trajectory is sharply separated from the threshold.

Appendix E Limitations

LARK provides a practical and theoretically motivated approach for trajectory-level selection in reasoning distillation. Its forward-pass score makes the method efficient to apply to large candidate pools, and the closed-form weighting rule avoids additional tuning while preserving the benefits of multi-trajectory supervision. The empirical results across multiple student models and benchmarks suggest that learnability is a useful principle for selecting reasoning trajectories.

There are two natural limitations of the present study. First, our experiments use a correctness-verified candidate pool, where all retained trajectories reach the correct final answer. This setting isolates the trajectory-selection problem from the separate problem of correctness verification, but future work could study LARK in noisier pools that include incorrect or partially correct teacher trajectories. Second, due to the computational cost of full-parameter SFT, our reported standard deviations are computed over independent decoding seeds while keeping the training configuration fixed. Running multiple independent SFT seeds would provide an even more complete estimate of training-time variance.
